Indicators.Remediation: Validate affected accountsCheck if the account is privileged or Tier-0Review recent password change activity (Event ID 4723 / 4724)Investigate suspicious behaviorLook for unusual LDAP or replication activityCheck for signs of DCShadow or unauthorized directory changesIdentify gaps or inconsistencies in logs around the change timeForce a secure password resetReset the password through standard administrative processesEnsure the change propagates correctly and resolves the mismatchReview domain controller integrityVerify only authorized systems are acting as domain controllersAudit replication permissions and privileged group membershipsMonitor and contain if neededRotate credentials for related accountsInvestigate lateral movement or persistence mechanismsIncrease monitoring on directory changes

Indicators.Name: Unexpected accounts in Cert Publishers group
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks to see if the Cert Publishers group contains members that aren't expected to be there.
Indicators.Remediation: After careful investigation, remove any accounts that do not belong from the Cert Publishers Group.

Indicators.Name: Built-in domain administrator account with old password (180 days)
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if the password of the built-in Domain Administrator account is older than 180 days.
Indicators.Remediation:
It is recommended to rotate the password on the built-in Administrator account every 180 days, or whenever there is the possibility that the password has become known or compromised.

The built-in Domain Administrator account is a well-known SID that is easily discoverable, regardless of attempts to obfuscate the account, such as renaming it.

Indicators.Name: AdminSDHolder object with inheritance enabled
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for inheritance enabled on the access control list (ACL) of the AdminSDHolder object.
Indicators.Remediation:
Any inheritance enabled on the AdminSDHolder object should be treated as highly suspicious unless there is clear, documented justification for it. If no planned change was authorized, escalate this as a potential indicator of compromise and initiate a broader Active Directory integrity investigation before making any changes.

Review the full ACL on the AdminSDHolder object and compare it against a known-good baseline. Identify any ACE entries that appear unexpected or overly permissive, paying particular attention to entries that grant write, modify ownership, or full control permissions to non-privileged or external accounts.

To disable inheritance on the AdminSDHolder object:

  1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers.
  2. In the top menu, select View and enable Advanced Features.
  3. Expand the domain, expand the System container, and locate the AdminSDHolder object.
  4. Right-click AdminSDHolder and select Properties.
  5. Navigate to the Security tab and select Advanced.
  6. In the Advanced Security Settings window, select Disable inheritance. When prompted, choose Convert inherited permissions into explicit permissions on this object.
  7. Review the resulting ACE list carefully and remove any entries that should not be present.

Indicators.Name: AdminSDHolder object with permission changes
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for modifications on the access control list (ACL) of the AdminSDHolder object.
Indicators.Remediation:
Organizations should investigate the permissions on the AdminSDHolder object if modified, and use attack path analysis software, such as Forest Druid, to analyze attack paths to privileged users in Active Directory.

Organizations, if changing the permissions on AdminSDHolder, should have an established process in place for awareness.

Any unplanned or undocumented changes should be treated as highly suspicious and must be investigated immediately. These events are a strong indicator of compromise and may point to an ongoing or previous breach of Active Directory.

Indicators.Name: Admins with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies administrator accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled, which exposes them to potential AS-REP Roasting attacks. These attacks allow adversaries to request encrypted authentication data from a domain controller and attempt to crack it offline, posing a serious risk when high-privilege accounts are affected.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that Kerberos pre-authentication is enabled for all user accounts, especially those with elevated privileges. If enabling pre-authentication is not feasible for a specific account, consider reducing its privileges to minimize potential impact if the account is compromised.

Indicators.Name: Built-in domain administrator account used within the last two weeks
Indicators.Description: The Domain Administrator account should only be used for initial build activities and, when necessary, disaster recovery. This indicator checks to see if the lastLogonTimestamp for the built-in Domain Administrator account has been updated within the last two weeks. If so, it could indicate that the user has been compromised.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that the built-in domain Administrator account is not used regularly and has a complex password known only to highly privileged admins.

Indicators.Name: Account with altSecurityIdentities configured
Indicators.Description: It is possible to add values to the altSecurityIdentities attribute and essentially impersonate that account. The altSecurityIdentities attribute is a multi-valued attribute used to create mappings for X.509 certificates and external Kerberos accounts. This indicator checks for accounts with the altSecurityIdentities attribute configured.
Indicators.Remediation: Remove any entries in altSecurityIdentities attributes that are not explicitly required.

Indicators.Name: Anonymous access to AD enabled
Indicators.Description: It is possible, though not recommended, to enable anonymous access to AD. This indicator looks for the presence of the flag that enables anonymous access. Anonymous access would allow unauthenticated users to query AD.
Indicators.Remediation: Disable anonymous access unless it is absolutely needed. The dsHeuristics attribute on the CN=Directory Service,CN=Windows NT,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=<forest_name> object should be set to disable anonymous access.

Indicators.Name: Anonymous NSPI access to AD enabled
Indicators.Description: Anonymous name service provider interface (NSPI) access on AD is a feature that allows anonymous RPC-based binds to AD. This indicator detects when NSPI access is enabled.
Indicators.Remediation: Disable anonymous name service provider interface (NSPI) access to AD unless it is absolutely needed. The dsHeuristics attribute on the CN=Directory Service,CN=Windows NT,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=<forest_name> object should be set to disable anonymous access.

Indicators.Name: Authenticated Users can add DNS records
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if the Authenticated Users group has the permission to create new DNS records in any DNS zone in the domain.
Indicators.Remediation:
Before removing the CreateChild permission from Authenticated Users, verify that the Domain Computers group (or an equivalent group covering all accounts expected to auto-register DNS records) already has the same permission on each affected zone. Removing the permission without a replacement will prevent domain-joined machines from auto-registering their DNS A records, which can cause name resolution and authentication failures across the domain.

To remediate each affected zone:

  1. Open DNS Manager (dnsmgmt.msc).
  2. Expand Forward Lookup Zones and locate the zone listed in the indicator results.
  3. Right-click the zone and select Properties, then open the Security tab.
  4. Click Add, enter Domain Computers, and grant it the Create all child objects permission. Click Apply.
  5. Select the Authenticated Users entry, uncheck Create all child objects, and click Apply and OK.
  6. Repeat for each zone listed in the indicator results.

To validate the change, re-run the indicator and confirm no zones are returned. You can also verify the ACL directly using dsacls "DC=<zonename>,CN=MicrosoftDNS,DC=DomainDnsZones,DC=<domain>,DC=<tld>" and confirm that Authenticated Users no longer holds the CreateChild permission.

Indicators.Name: Certificate template with SAN allowed
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if certificate templates are enabling requesters to specify a subjectAltName in the CSR.
Indicators.Remediation:
Review whether the identified templates genuinely require requesters to supply a SAN. The most common legitimate use case for this setting is for web server certificates where the DNS name must be specified at request time. If the template also carries an authentication EKU (such as Client Authentication or Smart Card Logon), this combination is highly dangerous and the SAN supply option must be disabled immediately. Additionally, check whether any certificates have already been issued from this template and consider whether rogue certificates need to be revoked.

To modify the SAN configuration on a certificate template:

  1. Open Certificate Templates Console (certtmpl.msc).
  2. Locate the flagged certificate template, right-click it, and select Properties.
  3. Navigate to the Subject Name tab.
  4. If Supply in the request is selected, change it to Build from this Active Directory information to prevent requesters from specifying arbitrary names.
  5. Select Apply and OK.

If the template must retain the SAN supply option for an operational reason, mitigate the risk by requiring CA certificate manager approval. To do this, navigate to the Issuance Requirements tab and enable CA certificate manager approval. This ensures all certificate requests are manually reviewed before issuance.

Indicators.Name: Certificate Authority with CertiGhost chase fallback enabled (CVE-2026-54121)
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) Certification Authorities that let a certificate request choose which Domain Controller the Certification Authority contacts during enrollment, instead of requiring a verified Domain Controller.
Indicators.Remediation:
Install the July 2026 security update on every host running the Certification Authority role. This is the recommended remediation: the update makes the CA validate that the chase target resolves to a legitimate Domain Controller before following it.

Where the update cannot be installed yet, clear the EDITF_ENABLECHASECLIENTDC bit on the CA host with certutil -setreg policy\EditFlags -EDITF_ENABLECHASECLIENTDC and restart the service with Restart-Service CertSvc -Force.

Treat that as an interim mitigation rather than a fix. Test it on a staging CA that mirrors your environment first and confirm that no legitimate enrollment relies on the chase fallback, because those requests fail once the bit is cleared. The bit can also be re-enabled by an administrator, a system image, or group policy, so monitor the value until the update is installed.

Indicators.Name: Changes to AD Display Specifiers in the past 90 days
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for changes made in the past 90 days to the adminContextMenu attribute on AD display specifiers. This attribute controls the right-click menus presented to users in the domain using MMC tools such as AD Users and Computers. Modifying these attributes can potentially allow attackers to get users to run arbitrary code if those menu options are clicked.
Indicators.Remediation: Review the changes and ensure they are legitimate. It is also recommended to revert write permissions on Display Specifiers to default state (only privileged users have write permissions).

Indicators.Name: Default security descriptor schema changes in the last 90 days
Indicators.Description: This indicator detects changes made to the default security descriptor schema in the last 90 days. If an attacker gets access to the schema instance in a given forest, they can make changes to the defaultSecurityDescriptor attribute on any AD object class. These changes would then propagate as new default Access Control Lists (ACLs) on any newly created object in AD, potentially weakening AD security posture.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that the changes to the SD schema are appropriate and valid, else investigate the cause and source of the changes.

Indicators.Name: Changes to Default Domain Policy or Default Domain Controllers Policy in the last 7 days
Indicators.Description: The Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controllers Policy GPOs are special objects within AD, and control domain-wide and Domain Controller wide security settings. This indicator looks for changes to these two special GPOs within the last 7 days.
Indicators.Remediation: Review the changes and ensure that any changes to these two GPOs have gone through well-known change processes and that any changes made to these GPOs are well-documented. Investigate any undocumented changes.

Indicators.Name: Computer account with older OS version
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for machine accounts running Windows Server 2012-R2, Windows 8.1, or older operating system versions.
Indicators.Remediation: Where possible, update servers and workstations to newer versions, which include improved security features.

Indicators.Name: Computer account with password last set over 90 days ago
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for computer accounts that have not rotated their passwords in the last 90 days. These passwords should be changed automatically every 30 days by default.
Indicators.Remediation:
Computers should change their passwords every 30 days, it should be investigated why they did not. Here are some suggestions to do to prevent it in the future:
  • Password Rotation: For each affected computer, initiate a manual password rotation process. Ensure that the new passwords are strong and comply with your organization's password policy.
  • Automated Password Rotation: Implement an automated password rotation solution or policy that aligns with industry best practices. Passwords should ideally be rotated every 30 days or according to your organization's security policies.
  • Review Password Policies: Evaluate your organization's password policies to ensure they enforce regular password rotations. Adjust these policies as needed to meet your security requirements.
Note: The 'Active' column shows if the account was active in the past 45 days.

References

Managed service accounts with passwords unchanged for more than 90 days | ANSSI

Indicators.Name: Domain Controller with old password
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for domain controller machine accounts whose password has not been reset in over 45 days. By default, machine accounts including DCs, automatically reset their passwords every 30 days. Any machine accounts with passwords older than that could indicate a DC that is no longer functioning in the domain.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that any DCs found by this indicator have a valid trust relationship with the domain and are properly replicating to partner domain controllers. Use repadmin /showrepl to test replication and run nltest /sc_verify to check for a secure channel connection to the domain.

Indicators.Name: Computer account in privileged group
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for computer accounts that are members of built-in privileged groups.
Indicators.Remediation: Check why those computer objects are members of privileged groups.

Indicators.Name: Computer with no password set
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for computer objects that did not join the domain and most likely have no password set.
Indicators.Remediation:
System administrators should review and remove any unused or stale pre-created computer accounts in Active Directory. Alternatively, administrators can use the “Reset Account” option in the Active Directory Users and Computers (ADUC) console to reset the password for a computer object.

Note that when resetting the password of a computer account configured as a pre–Windows 2000 system, the new password will not change and will stay as the lowercase version of the computer's name. To change pre-Windows 2000 computer accounts password, you should set their password manually.

To reduce the attack surface and prevent misuse, ensure all computer accounts are actively managed, monitored, and tied to legitimate, joined machines.

Indicators.Name: Account with SPN that has unconstrained delegation
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for computer or user accounts with SPN that are trusted for unconstrained Kerberos delegation. These accounts store users' Kerberos TGT locally to authenticate to other systems on their behalf. Computers and users trusted with unconstrained delegation are good targets for Kerberos-based attacks.
Indicators.Remediation: Accounts that require Kerberos delegation should be set to constrain that delegation to the particular service or services that require delegation. Attempts should be made to have Kerberos-enabled accounts not be privileged accounts.

Indicators.Name: Account with Kerberos constrained delegation configured to AZUREADSSOACC
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for accounts that have constrained delegation configured to the SSO computer account, AZUREADSSOACC.
Indicators.Remediation:
As there is no functional reason to allow constrained delegation to the SSO computer account, it is recommended to remove this configuration for increased security.

Kerberos constrained delegation is configured on the msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo attribute of the source account. The attribute contains a list of destination SPNs that delegation is allowed to.

To view this configuration and remove the insecure SSO SPNs, perform the following steps:

  1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc), and check the Advanced Features option under View.
  2. Navigate to the location of the detected account(s) and double-click it to view its properties.
  3. Click the Delegation tab and check the Expanded option.
  4. Locate the SPNs detected by the indicator, then select and remove them. The indicator displays only SPNs of the SSO computer account.
    • In case all the SPNs displayed were detected by the indicator, select the "Do not trust this computer for delegation" option to remove them all, and click Apply.

Alternatively, if the Delegation tab does not show all SPNs or if the indicator still shows results after removing them, you can view and edit the msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo attribute directly within the Attribute Editor tab of the detected account.

Indicators.Name: Account with constrained delegation configured to krbtgt
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for accounts that have constrained delegation configured to the KRBTGT account.
Indicators.Remediation:
There is no legitimate use case for constrained delegation configured to the KRBTGT account. If this indicator fires in a production environment that is not undergoing a scheduled penetration test, it must be treated as a high-confidence indicator of compromise. Initiate an Active Directory integrity investigation before removing the delegation to ensure the breadth of the intrusion is understood.

To remove the constrained delegation from the identified account:

  1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers and enable Advanced Features under the View menu.
  2. Locate the flagged account, right-click it, and select Properties.
  3. Navigate to the Delegation tab.
  4. Select Do not trust this computer for delegation to remove all delegation settings.
  5. Select Apply and OK.

Indicators.Name: Dangerous trust attribute set
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies trusts set with either TRUST_ATTRIBUTE_CROSS_ORGANIZATION_ENABLE_TGT_DELEGATION or TRUST_ATTRIBUTE_PIM_TRUST. These bits will either allow a kerberos ticket to be delegated or reduce the protection that SID Filtering provides.
Indicators.Remediation: Confirm that the trust attributes are configured as desired.

Indicators.Name: Domain controller with Print Spooler service remotely accessible
Indicators.Description:
This indicator tests whether the Print Spooler service is remotely accessible on domain controllers. A DC where remote access to the Print Spooler has been blocked through hardening will not be flagged by this indicator, as the underlying attack surface has been eliminated.

This indicator requires the local server to be running the Print Spooler service to function or it will return Failed to run.
Indicators.Remediation:
There are two remediation options. The preferred option where local printing must be preserved is to harden the Print Spooler by blocking remote access — consult Microsoft guidance for the appropriate registry or policy setting for your Windows version. Alternatively, if the DC does not need to print locally, disable the service entirely.

To disable the Print Spooler service on the identified domain controller:

  1. Open Services (services.msc) on the DC, or connect to it remotely via the Services snap-in in Computer Management.
  2. Locate the Print Spooler service.
  3. Right-click the service and select Stop to immediately halt the service.
  4. Right-click again and select Properties. Set the Startup type to Disabled.
  5. Select Apply and OK.

To enforce this at scale across all DCs, configure a Group Policy Object linked to the Domain Controllers OU: navigate to Computer Configuration > Preferences > Control Panel Settings > Services, and set the Print Spooler service startup type to Disabled.

Indicators.Name: Suspicion of DCShadow activity
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for computer objects that appear to be acting like domain controllers but are not configured as legitimate domain controllers. Such objects may indicate DCShadow activity or rogue domain controller registration.
Indicators.Remediation:
Treat this finding as an active compromise. Engage an incident response team and do not attempt remediation without a full scope assessment, as premature actions can destroy forensic evidence.

To investigate the scope of the attack:

  1. Confirm whether the object is related to a recent legitimate domain controller promotion, configuration change, or lifecycle operation before making changes.
  2. Review the AD replication metadata for recently modified objects. Use repadmin /showattr * DC=domain,DC=com /atts:* /filter:"(objectClass=*)" /long to identify unexpected attribute changes.
  3. Check AD Sites and Services for any rogue or unrecognized server objects that may have been registered as a DC during the attack window and remove them.
  4. Review recently modified privileged group memberships, SID history attributes, and delegation settings on high-value accounts for unauthorized changes.
  5. Identify the source workstation and user account used to perform the attack, disable the account, and isolate the workstation from the network.
  6. After scoping, revert all malicious attribute changes and perform a full Active Directory integrity assessment to ensure no additional persistence mechanisms were established.

Indicators.Name: Account with constrained delegation configured to ghost SPN
Indicators.Description: When computers are decommissioned, delegation configuration to them is often not cleaned up. Such a delegation could allow an attacker that has the privileges to write to the ServicePrincipalName attribute of another service account, to escalate privileges on those services. This could result in escalating privileges by moving laterally across the infrastructure. This indicator looks for accounts that have Constrained Delegation configured to ghost SPNs.
Indicators.Remediation: Remove any Kerberos delegations to ghost SPN(s).

Indicators.Name: Risky delegated permission on AD OUs
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies Organizational Units (OUs) in Active Directory that have been delegated powerful permissions, which could lead to security risks or unauthorized privilege escalation.
Indicators.Remediation:
Review the permissions granted to each Organizational Unit (OU) in Active Directory, particularly looking at any special rights that may have been delegated. This includes permissions that allow restoring deleted objects, overriding password expiration, or migrating user identities.

These advanced permissions, known as "Extended Rights", are not visible in the standard Active Directory graphical tools such as Active Directory Users and Computers (ADUC). As a result, reviewing and removing them typically requires the use of scripting tools such as PowerShell, or assistance from your IT or security team.

To remove these permissions, administrators can use PowerShell scripts to inspect and modify access control entries (ACEs) on Organizational Units. For example, the following script snippet demonstrates how to view which OU has the Reanimate_Tombstone right:

Get-Acl -Path "AD:OU=TargetOU,DC=domain,DC=com" | ForEach-Object { $_.Access | Where-Object { $_.ObjectType -eq '4c164200-20c0-11d0-a768-00aa006e0529' } }

This kind of action should only be performed by experienced administrators, and ideally through a change management process. If you are not familiar with PowerShell or Active Directory delegation, contact your IT or security team to review and remove unnecessary rights safely.

Indicators.Name: Privileged user disabled
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for privileged user accounts, as indicated by their adminCount attribute set to 1, that are disabled. If a privileged account is disabled, it should be removed from its privileged group(s) to prevent inadvertent misuse.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that privileged groups have only necessary users as members.

Indicators.Name: OU with excessive permission enabling BadSuccessor dMSA escalation
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for excessive permissions to create delegated Managed Service Accounts (dMSAs) within Active Directory organizational units (OU) or NC head (NC Head is the top-level object of a Naming Context (NC) in Active Directory) across domains that contain Windows Server 2025 domain controllers. The indicator identifies non-privileged identities that have been granted CreateChild, GenericAll, WriteDACL, or WriteOwner permissions on OUs or NC head, which could enable the execution of the "BadSuccessor" Privilege Escalation attack. The "BadSuccessor" attack is a technique which exploits vulnerabilities in Microsoft's Active Directory and enables domain takeover. The attack leverages a feature called Delegated Managed Service Accounts (dMSA), which was introduced in Windows Server 2025.
Indicators.Remediation:
Limit the ability to create delegated Managed Service Accounts (dMSAs) by applying the principle of least privilege. Ensure only highly privileged and appropriately monitored administrative accounts have permissions to create dMSAs across the domain. To modify OU or NC head permissions, open Active Directory Users and Computers (ADUC), right-click the relevant object, select "Security," and remove the vulnerable permissions from the affected users. Enumerate all non-default principals with dMSA creation permissions and identify the organizational units or NC head where these permissions are granted. Thoroughly review the output to determine if each identity requires this level of access and remove unnecessary permissions from the corresponding OU Access Control Lists (ACLs).

Before implementing any permission changes, test modifications in a controlled environment to ensure proper functionality of existing services and avoid unintended disruptions to domain operations.

Note on patch availability: Microsoft has released a security update addressing the BadSuccessor vulnerability (CVE-2025-53779). However, this indicator is unable to verify whether the patch has been applied to your domain controllers. If you have confirmed that all Windows Server 2025 domain controllers in your environment are fully patched, individual results reported by this indicator can be added to the exclusion list to prevent them from affecting your score.

Indicators.Name: Unsecured DNS configuration
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for DNS zones configured with ZONE_UPDATE_UNSECURE, which allows updating a DNS record anonymously.
Indicators.Remediation: Reconfigure DNS zones to only allow secure updates using the following command: dnscmd <servername> /Config <zone> /AllowUpdate 2

Indicators.Name: DNS zone transfer allowed to any host
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for DNS zones configured to allow unrestricted zone transfer requests.
Indicators.Remediation:
Review DNS server debug logs or network traffic captures to determine whether any unauthorized AXFR requests have already been made against the exposed zones. If zone data has been exfiltrated, assume the attacker has a complete picture of the internal network and treat the exposure accordingly in any ongoing incident response activities.

To restrict zone transfers to authorized DNS servers only, use one of the following approaches:

  • In DNS Manager, right-click the affected zone and select Properties. Navigate to the Zone Transfers tab and select Only to servers listed on the Name Servers tab.
  • Alternatively, to specify a custom list of authorized servers, select Only to the following servers and add the IP addresses of the authorized secondary DNS servers.

For Active Directory-integrated zones, ensure the replication scope and permissions are correctly configured to prevent unintended access.

Important Disclaimer

When configuring zone transfers in DNS Manager, if Only to the following servers is selected, do not add the DSP server to the list. Doing so will cause the indicator to generate a false positive, incorrectly reporting that the zone allows transfer to any host.

Indicators.Name: Domain Controller in inconsistent state
Indicators.Description:
This indicator looks for Domain Controllers that may be in an inconsistent state, indicating a possible rogue or otherwise non-functional DC. DCs in a consistent state are characterized by the following:

  1. UserAccountControl attribute on the DC machine object has the SERVER_TRUST_ACCOUNT flag set.
  2. A corresponding object of type server exists for the DC in the configuration partition.
  3. That server object must have a child NTDS Settings object of type nTDSDSA.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that all DCs within your environment are healthy and functional. It is not uncommon for attackers to attempt to stand up "fake" DCs; however, these DCs are generally distinguishable from real DCs by the metadata found by this security indicator.

Indicators.Name: Domain Controller owner is not an administrator
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for Domain Controller computer accounts whose owner is not a Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, or built-in Administrator account.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that only privileged Tier 0 admin accounts and the domain's built-in groups, such as Enterprise Admins, Domain Admins, and Administrators, have ownership of Domain Controller computer objects. Any unrecognized owner may be a sign of compromise.

Indicators.Name: Domain with obsolete functional level
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for AD domains that have a domain functional level set to Windows Server 2012 R2 or lower. These lower functional levels mean that newer security features available in AD cannot be leveraged. If the OS version of your domain controllers supports it, you should update to a newer domain functional level to take full advantage of security advancements in AD.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that your AD domains are running at the highest functional level available for your OS version to ensure access to the latest security improvements. Also, consider upgrading the OS to 2016 or above, as new functional levels are available.

Indicators.Name: Non-default access to DPAPI key
Indicators.Description: This indicator uses API calls to check whether each DC has non-default principals permitted to retrieve the domain DPAPI backup key (using LsaRetrievePrivateData).
Indicators.Remediation: These permissions allow a principal to use LsaRetrievePrivateData to retrieve the domain DPAPI backup keys. Review these principals, investigate and remove any unneeded permissions using adsiedit.msc or the ldp utility.

Indicators.Name: Operator group no longer protected by AdminSDHolder and SDProp
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if dwAdminSDExMask mask on dsHeuristics has been set, which indicates a change to the SDProp behavior that could compromise security. Certain groups can be removed from SDProp protection with this setting.
Indicators.Remediation: Set dwAdminSDExMask flag (16th byte) on dsHeuristics to 0 or SDProp (AdminSDHolder) behavior will not fully apply to Operator groups.

Indicators.Name: Microsoft service principal with suspicious credentials
Indicators.Description:
This indicator checks if certain Microsoft service principals have secrets assigned to them.

Required permissions

  • Application.Read.All
Indicators.Remediation:
Microsoft has patched the underlying vulnerability that enabled these hidden permissions. However, the presence of credentials on these service principals has no legitimate justification and may indicate that an attacker already exploited the exposure. Consider this finding an indicator of suspicious activity requiring investigation.

To investigate whether the credentials were used maliciously, review the Entra audit and sign-in logs for the identified service principal:

  1. Open the Microsoft Entra admin center.
  2. Expand Identity, expand Monitoring & health, and select Audit logs.
  3. Filter by Service: Core Directory and search for the service principal's display name or Object ID in the Target field. Look for any role assignment operations, credential additions, or policy modifications performed by or targeting this principal.
  4. Navigate to Sign-in logs and filter by the service principal's Application ID to identify any OAuth token issuances using client credentials. Note the timestamps, IP addresses, and resource targets of any token requests.
  5. If suspicious activity is found, correlate the timestamps with other privileged operations in the tenant - such as Global Administrator role assignments or Conditional Access policy changes - to assess the full scope of potential compromise.

Regardless of investigation findings, remove any credentials assigned to the identified Microsoft service principals, as there is no valid operational reason for them to exist.

Indicators.Name: Unresolved Entra ID privileged role member
Indicators.Description:
This indicator identifies privileged role assignments where the member cannot be found, either due to deleted eligible users or GDAP partner relationships.

Required permissions

  • RoleManagement.Read.All
  • Directory.Read.All
Indicators.Remediation:
To address ununresolved privileged role members, follow these steps based on the scenario:

For Deleted Users:

  1. Navigate to the Microsoft Entra admin center
  2. Use the provided UserPrincipalName and DisplayName to search in the Users blade
  3. If confirmed as deleted, remove their role eligibility through PIM

For GDAP Partner Relationships:

  1. Access the Microsoft Admin Center (direct link)
  2. Review all partner relationships and their associated role assignments
  3. Verify that each partner relationship is legitimate and necessary

Note: GDAP relationships cannot be viewed through Graph API from the managed tenant, but are visible in the admin portal to Global Administrators

Regular review of both scenarios is recommended as part of your security governance process.

Indicators.Name: Admin account enabled but inactive
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for admin accounts that are enabled, but have not logged in for the past 90 days. Attackers who can compromise these accounts may be able to operate unnoticed.
Indicators.Remediation: Admin accounts that are not in use should be removed or disabled.

Indicators.Name: Enterprise Key Admins with full access to the domain
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for evidence of a bug in certain versions of Windows Server 2016 Adprep that grants undue access to the Enterprise Key Admins group.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that users don't have unnecessary permissions.

Indicators.Name: Ephemeral admin
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for users which were added and removed from an admin group within a 48-hour window. Such short-lived accounts may indicate malicious activity.
Indicators.Remediation: Confirm that any additions/removals from admin groups are valid and properly accounted for.

Indicators.Name: ADCS ESC11 - Certificate Authority with no RPC encryption enforcement
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) Certificate Authorities that do not enforce RPC encryption for certificate enrollment requests. It checks whether the CA has the IF_ENFORCEENCRYPTICERTREQUEST interface flag disabled, allowing certificate requests over an RPC interface that does not require packet privacy.
Indicators.Remediation:
To mitigate ESC11, ensure that the Certificate Authority (CA) enforces encrypted and integrity-protected RPC certificate enrollment requests. This is controlled by the IF_ENFORCEENCRYPTICERTREQUEST flag, which requires the CA's RPC interface to use packet encryption.

Interface flags are stored in the Windows Registry for each Certificate Authority (CA). To check the current InterfaceFlags value to verify if IF_ENFORCEENCRYPTICERTREQUEST is set, run the certutil command on the AD CS server:

certutil -getreg CA\InterfaceFlags

If the output does not include IF_ENFORCEENCRYPTICERTREQUEST (0x200) in the flags, RPC encryption is not enforced.

Enable the IF_ENFORCEENCRYPTICERTREQUEST flag on the Certificate Authority server: certutil -setreg CA\InterfaceFlags +IF_ENFORCEENCRYPTICERTREQUEST, followed by restarting the Certificate Services service using net stop certsvc & net start certsvc.

Important: Before implementing this change in a production environment, thoroughly test it in a controlled lab to ensure it does not disrupt certificate enrollment processes or other CA operations. Enforcing encrypted RPC certificate requests may prevent older or non-compliant clients from enrolling certificates (such as Windows XP or older non-Windows systems) from enrolling certificates. If compatibility issues arise, consider upgrading legacy systems rather than leaving the CA vulnerable to NTLM relay attacks.

Indicators.Name: ADCS ESC13 - certificate template with issuance policy linked to group
Indicators.Description: This indicator finds published certificate templates that contain group-linked issuance policy extensions, making them susceptible to the ESC13 abuse technique.
Indicators.Remediation:
If the OID group link configuration is not needed, remove it:

  1. Open ADSI Edit (adsiedit.msc).
  2. Navigate to the location of the relevant issuance policy, provided in the results as PolicyDN.
  3. Right-click the object and select Properties.
  4. Select the Attribute Editor tab, locate the msDS-OIDToGroupLink attribute, and double-click it to edit.
  5. Select Clear, then confirm with OK and Apply.

If using templates linked to groups is required, it's recommended to restrict enrollment rights to the minimum possible set of principals. In case the linked group is privileged, enrollment rights should be limited to only Tier Zero principals.

Finally, consider enabling "CA certificate manager approval" (within the "Issuance Requirements" tab of the certificate template). This requires a CA administrator to approve enrollment requests before the CA issues a certificate, adding an additional layer of security.

Indicators.Name: ADCS ESC14 - weak certificate mapping
Indicators.Description:
This indicator detects certificate templates that are vulnerable to ESC14 due to misconfigured explicit certificate mappings using the altSecurityIdentities attribute. AltSecurityIdentities is a multi-valued Active Directory attribute used to map X.509 certificates to user accounts for certificate-based authentication. Some mapping formats are considered strong, while others are weak and prone to abuse.

An IOE will be found in case there are published certificate templates with:

  • Schema v1 templates with CT_FLAG_SUBJECT_ALT_REQUIRE_EMAIL or CT_FLAG_SUBJECT_ALT_REQUIRE_DNS
  • OR templates with:
    • CT_FLAG_SUBJECT_ALT_REQUIRE_DOMAIN_DNS
    • CT_FLAG_SUBJECT_ALT_REQUIRE_DNS
    • CT_FLAG_SUBJECT_ALT_REQUIRE_UPN
    • CT_FLAG_SUBJECT_ALT_REQUIRE_SPN
  • With client authentication EKUs (Any Purpose, PKINIT, Smart Card Logon, or Client Authentication)

This indicator covers multiple ESC14 attack variants:

  • ESC14B: Weak certificate mapping based on target's X509RFC822 attribute.
  • ESC14C: Weak certificate mapping based on target's issuer and subject attribute.
  • ESC14D: Weak certificate mapping based on target's subject attribute.
Indicators.Remediation:
Before making changes, identify all accounts currently using the altSecurityIdentities attribute and assess whether any weak mapping formats or unauthorized mappings exist. To do this, run the following command on a domain controller:

Get-ADObject -Filter {altSecurityIdentities -like "*"} -Properties altSecurityIdentities, distinguishedName

Review the output for any entries using weak mapping formats (X509RFC822, X509IssuerSubject, X509SubjectOnly) or for any mappings pointing to certificates not issued to the intended account owner.

Note: Microsoft began denying weak explicit mappings following the installation of KB5014754 (September 9, 2025). If this update is installed on all domain controllers, weak explicit mapping abuse is blocked. However, ESC14 remains exploitable if an attacker has write access to the altSecurityIdentities attribute, as they can still add strong mappings to compromise other accounts.

To replace weak mappings with strong ones:

  1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers and enable Advanced Features under the View menu.
  2. Locate the affected user account, right-click it, and select Properties.
  3. Navigate to the Attribute Editor tab and locate the altSecurityIdentities attribute.
  4. Double-click the attribute, remove any weak mapping entries, and replace them with strong formats such as:
    • X509:<SKI> - cryptographic hash of the certificate's public key
    • X509:<SHA1-PUKEY> - SHA-1 hash of the certificate's public key
    • X509:<I><SR> - certificate issuer DN combined with the serial number
  5. Select OK, then Apply to save changes.

Additionally, enforce strong certificate binding on all domain controllers by setting the registry value HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Kdc\StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement to 2. This ensures Kerberos authentication rejects weak or manipulated certificate-to-account mappings.

Finally, restrict write permissions on the altSecurityIdentities attribute to only those principals that legitimately require full administrative control over user or computer accounts.

Indicators.Name: ADCS ESC15 - Schema 1 vulnerability
Indicators.Description: This indicator detects configurations that enable the ADCS ESC15 attack (also known as EKUwu, CVE-2024-49019), which abuses certificate templates with Schema Version 1 to allow requesters to inject arbitrary Application Policy OIDs (Extended Key Usages) into their certificate signing requests.
Indicators.Remediation:
Before remediating, check whether any certificates have already been issued from the identified vulnerable templates that may have been used maliciously. Review the CA's issued certificates log in the Certification Authority console (certsrv.msc) and look for any certificates with unexpected Application Policy extensions or EKUs inconsistent with the template's intended purpose.

ESC15 affects all Schema Version 1 templates with the Supply in the request subject name setting, including commonly deployed defaults such as WebServer, ExchangeUser, ExchangeUserSignature, CEPEncryption, and OfflineRouter. To remediate:

  1. Identify all Schema Version 1 templates by reviewing the Certificate Templates console or querying AD for templates with mspki-template-schema-version=1.
  2. Review enrollment permissions on each template. Remove enrollment rights for broad non-privileged groups such as Authenticated Users or Domain Users from any template that should only be accessible to administrators.
  3. For templates no longer in use, unpublish or delete them entirely from the Certification Authority console. Templates not published by any CA cannot be exploited.
  4. For templates still in use, upgrade them to Schema Version 2 by duplicating the template in the Certificate Templates console. The duplicate will automatically be created as Schema Version 2, which is not vulnerable to ESC15.
  5. If an immediate upgrade is not possible, disable the requestor-supplied Application Policy capability using ADSI Edit by setting the msPKI-Certificate-Name-Flag attribute to 0 on the affected template object in AD.

After applying changes, request a test certificate with modified EKUs to verify that the template no longer accepts arbitrary application policy values. A properly remediated CA will reject requests with unauthorized application policies.

Note on patch availability: Microsoft has released a security update addressing the ESC15 vulnerability (CVE-2024-49019). However, this indicator is unable to verify whether the patch has been applied to your certification authorities. If you have confirmed that all Active Directory certificate services servers in your environment are fully patched, individual results reported by this indicator can be added to the exclusion list to prevent them from affecting your score.

Indicators.Name: ADCS ESC16 - Certificate Authority with globally disabled security extension
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) Certificate Authorities that are configured to globally disable the SID security extension (szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT) by including OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2 in the CA's policy\DisableExtensionList. This configuration causes the CA to omit the SID security extension from all issued certificates, regardless of individual template configuration.
Indicators.Remediation:
Review the Certificate Authority configuration and ensure that the SID security extension szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT, OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.311.25.2 is not listed in the CA's policy\DisableExtensionList. If present, remove this OID.

Because this setting affects all certificates issued by the CA, validate the change in a controlled test or staging environment before applying it in production. Some legacy systems or authentication flows may depend on older certificate behavior.

In addition, ensure that domain controllers are configured to enforce strong certificate mapping by setting StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement to full enforcement. You can do it by configuring the registry value to 2 on all DCs: reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Kdc /v StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement /t REG_DWORD /d 2 /f

After setting this value, restart the Key Distribution Center (KDC) service or reboot the domain controller for the change to take effect.

This prevents fallback to weak mapping methods even if a certificate is missing the SID extension.

Indicators.Name: ADCS ESC1 - Enrollee Supplies Subject with Authentication EKU
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if certificate templates in the forest meet all of the following conditions - Manager approval is disabled, No authorized signatures are required, "Supply in request" is allowed and Authentication EKU present.
Indicators.Remediation:
Multiple actions can be taken to ensure certificate templates will be less vulnerable:
  1. Enable manager approval - make sure manager approval is enabled and required on the certificate, and approve each request manually after inspecting it.
  2. No authorized signatures are required - it is recommended to set it to 1 so that each request will have to be signed by an authorized certificate.
  3. SAN Enabled - evaluate if the certificate needs to specify a subjectAltName, if not disable this option.
  4. Authentication EKU present - make sure the certificate template is being used for authentication only.
    For example, a certificate that is solely used for code signing should not also be used for authentication.

Indicators.Name: ADCS ESC2 - Certificate template with Any Purpose EKU or no EKU
Indicators.Description: This indicator detects published certificate templates that are vulnerable to the ADCS ESC2 attack. A template is flagged when all of the following conditions are met: manager approval is disabled, no authorized signatures (issuance requirements) are required, and the template either explicitly contains the Any Purpose EKU (OID 2.5.29.37.0) or defines no EKU at all. In addition, at least one non-privileged principal must hold enrollment rights on the template.
Indicators.Remediation:
If you have a Certification Authority installed, you can manage certificate templates using the Certificate Templates console (certtmpl.msc). To open it:

Open Certification Authority by typing certsrv.msc in the Start menu search bar or in the Run dialog (Win+R), right-click on Certificate templates and choose Manage. Then right click a template and choose Properties.

Before remediating, review the CA's issued certificates log in the Certification Authority console (certsrv.msc) for any certificates issued from the flagged templates that may have been misused. Revoke any suspicious certificates.

  1. Remove the Any Purpose EKU — open the Certificate Templates console (certtmpl.msc), edit the template, navigate to the Extensions tab, and replace the Any Purpose EKU with the minimum set of specific EKUs the template actually requires (for example, Client Authentication only).
  2. Define explicit EKUs — if the template has no EKU defined, add one or more specific EKUs matching the template's intended purpose. A template with no EKU is functionally equivalent to Any Purpose and should always carry explicit restrictions.
  3. Enable manager approval — on the Issuance Requirements tab, enable CA certificate manager approval so that all enrollment requests require manual review before a certificate is issued.
  4. Require authorized signatures — set the number of authorized signatures to at least 1 and specify the required issuance policy or application policy, so that requests must be countersigned by an existing authorized certificate.
  5. Restrict enrollment rights — remove Enroll or AutoEnroll permissions from broad groups such as Domain Users, Authenticated Users, and Everyone. Grant enrollment rights only to specific, named principals with a documented business need.
  6. Unpublish unused templates — if the template is no longer required, remove it from all Certificate Authorities in certsrv.msc and, if appropriate, delete it from the Certificate Templates container.

Indicators.Name: ADCS ESC3 - Enrollment Agent certificate
Indicators.Description: This indicator detects certificate templates vulnerable to the ADCS ESC3 attack, which exploits Enrollment Agent (Certificate Request Agent) templates to enable unauthorized certificate issuance on behalf of other domain users. ESC3 is a two-stage attack that requires two complementary misconfigured templates working together.
Indicators.Remediation:
Before remediating, review the CA's issued certificates log in the Certification Authority console (certsrv.msc) for any certificates issued via Enrollment Agent signatures against authentication templates. If found, those certificates may have been used to impersonate domain users and should be revoked immediately.

ESC3 involves two types of vulnerable templates that require different remediation approaches.

For Enrollment Agent templates (Certificate Request Agent EKU)

  1. Identify all templates with the Certificate Request Agent EKU (OID: 1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.1). The built-in EnrollmentAgent template is commonly vulnerable.
  2. Remove enrollment rights for broad non-privileged groups such as Domain Users, Authenticated Users, or Everyone. Enrollment agent privileges should only be granted to specific, trusted service accounts with documented business requirements.
  3. Enable CA certificate manager approval on these templates to add human oversight to all Enrollment Agent certificate requests.
  4. If the template is no longer needed, unpublish it from all Certificate Authorities or delete it entirely.

For templates accepting Enrollment Agent signatures

  1. Identify templates that accept enrollment agent signatures for authentication. Common examples include the default User template (especially Schema Version 1) and custom templates with authorized signature requirements.
  2. For Schema Version 1 templates, upgrade to Version 2 by duplicating the template in the Certificate Templates console.
  3. Enable CA certificate manager approval for high-value templates that permit authentication EKUs.

Configure CA-level Enrollment Agent restrictions

The most effective mitigation is to configure enrollment agent restrictions at the CA level, which limits which users can act as enrollment agents and which templates they can request certificates for. To configure this:

  1. Open the Certification Authority console (certsrv.msc).
  2. Right-click the CA and select Properties.
  3. Navigate to the Enrollment Agents tab and configure restrictions to specify which users or groups can act as enrollment agents, which templates they can request, and which accounts they can enroll on behalf of.

Even if vulnerable templates remain published, properly configured CA-level restrictions will prevent exploitation of ESC3.

Indicators.Name: ADCS ESC4 - risky control paths expose certificate templates
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for non-default principals with the ability to write properties on published certificate templates.
Indicators.Remediation: Unprivileged users should not be able to write properties on published certificate templates. Doing so potentially gives them the ability to escalate their access and create vulnerable certificates to enroll. Remove unnecessary permissions from the certificate template.

Indicators.Name: ADCS ESC5 - PKI object with vulnerable ACL
Indicators.Description:
This indicator identifies Active Directory Certificate Services (ADCS) objects with overly permissive Access Control Lists (ACLs). When non-administrative principals have dangerous write permissions on these PKI objects, they can modify security-critical configurations to enable privilege escalation attacks.

This indicator covers multiple ESC5 attack variants:

  • ESC 5A: Vulnerable Certificate Templates container permissions
  • ESC 5B: Vulnerable CA object permissions (Enrollment Services)
  • ESC 5C: Vulnerable NTAuthCertificates container permissions
Indicators.Remediation:
Remove or restrict dangerous write permissions on all PKI objects, including Certificate Authority container and objects, Certificate Templates container, Enrollment Services Container, and NTAuthCertificates container. Only privileged administrative groups should have these permissions.

Remediation Steps
  1. Review Identified ACLs: Examine each principal with dangerous permissions and determine if the access is necessary. Pay special attention to NTAuthCertificates container permissions, as these are the most critical.
  2. Remove Excessive Permissions:
    • dsacls: dsacls "AD_OBJECT_DN" /R "PRINCIPAL"
    • PowerShell: $dn="AD_DN"; $acl=Get-Acl "AD:$dn"; $acl.Access | ?{$_.IdentityReference -eq 'PRINCIPAL'} | %{$acl.RemoveAccessRule($_)}; Set-Acl "AD:$dn" $acl
  3. Apply Principle of Least Privilege: Grant only the minimum necessary permissions. If a group needs to view templates, grant Read permissions only.
  4. Audit Regularly: Implement periodic reviews of PKI object ACLs to detect configuration drift.

Indicators.Name: ADCS ESC7 - non-privileged account with Manage CA or Manage Certificates permission
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) Certificate Authorities where non-privileged principals are granted high-impact administrative permissions. Specifically, it checks for accounts that are not considered highly privileged but have been assigned the ManageCA or ManageCertificates access rights on a Certificate Authority.
Indicators.Remediation:
Review Certificate Authority permissions and remove ManageCA and ManageCertificates rights from non-privileged accounts. These permissions should only be granted to dedicated PKI administrators.

To remediate using the Certificate Authority management console:

  1. Open the Certification Authority management console (certsrv.msc) on the CA server, or from a workstation with the appropriate administrative tools installed.
  2. Right-click the Certificate Authority name and select Properties.
  3. Navigate to the Security tab.
  4. Review all users and groups listed.
  5. For each non-privileged principal, remove the Manage CA and/or Issue and Manage Certificates permissions. Fully remove the principal only if it should have no access to the CA.
  6. Click OK to apply the changes.
  7. Repeat for all Certificate Authorities in the environment.

After remediation, confirm that no non-privileged users or broad groups retain these permissions, including via nested group membership.

Indicators.Name: ADCS ESC8 - AD Certificate Authority with Web Enrollment
Indicators.Description:
This indicator identifies Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) servers that expose a vulnerable Web Enrollment endpoint by allowing NTLM authentication without enforcing Enhanced Protection for Authentication (EPA). The indicator enumerates Certificate Authorities (CAs) from the Enrollment Services container in each domain's configuration partition and tests their web enrollment endpoints over HTTP. During the test, it simulates a full NTLM handshake and determines whether EPA is enforced.

A result of IoE Found indicates that a CA's Web Enrollment endpoint accepts NTLM authentication and does not enforce EPA, leaving it vulnerable to credential relay attacks such as ESC8. A result of Passed means the endpoint either requires EPA, does not support NTLM, or only supports Kerberos, all of which are considered secure configurations. The test runs only once per CA host, even if the CA is referenced by multiple domains. Each output record includes a list of affected domains where the vulnerable CA was discovered.

The indicator will Fail to Run (no impact on posture score) if none of the CA endpoints could be evaluated. This occurs when all discovered servers meet one of the following conditions:

  • Cannot Resolve - The CA hostname could not be resolved to an IP address.
  • Unreachable - The host is resolvable, but the Web Enrollment service could not be contacted.
Indicators.Remediation:
The primary remediation is to enforce Enhanced Protection for Authentication (EPA) on the IIS web application hosting the AD CS Web Enrollment endpoint. To do this on the CA server:

  1. Open IIS Manager (inetmgr) on the CA server.
  2. In the Connections pane, expand the server node and navigate to Sites > Default Web Site > CertSrv.
  3. In the Features View, double-click Authentication.
  4. Right-click Windows Authentication and select Providers. Ensure Negotiate is listed above NTLM. Remove NTLM from the providers list if NTLM is not required.
  5. Right-click Windows Authentication and select Advanced Settings. Set Extended Protection to Required.
  6. Select OK and perform an IIS Reset (iisreset) to apply the changes.

Additionally, enable HTTPS on the Web Enrollment endpoint and ensure clients connect only via HTTPS, as EPA is only effective over a protected channel. If the Web Enrollment role is not actively in use, remove it entirely via Server Manager to eliminate the attack surface.

If NTLM cannot be eliminated from the environment, restrict which machines are allowed to connect to the CA Web Enrollment interface via Windows Firewall or network-level controls, limiting access to only authorized management systems.

Indicators.Name: ADCS ESC9 - no security extension
Indicators.Description: This indicator detects certificate templates vulnerable to ADCS ESC9, which exploits templates configured to omit the SID security extension (szOID_NTDS_CA_SECURITY_EXT). Templates with the CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION flag (0x80000) in msPKI-Enrollment-Flag do not include this extension in issued certificates, preventing SID-based authentication validation introduced in the May 2022 patch (CVE-2022-26923).
Indicators.Remediation:
Before remediating, review the CA's issued certificates log in the Certification Authority console (certsrv.msc) for any certificates recently issued from the flagged templates. If suspicious issuances are found, revoke those certificates immediately and investigate whether they were used to authenticate as privileged accounts.

To remediate, apply the following steps:

  1. Remove the CT_FLAG_NO_SECURITY_EXTENSION flag from all affected templates by clearing bit 0x80000 from the template's msPKI-Enrollment-Flag attribute. Use the following PowerShell command on a domain controller:

$template = Get-ADObject -Identity "CN=TemplateName,CN=Certificate Templates,CN=Public Key Services,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=yourdomain,DC=com" -Properties msPKI-Enrollment-Flag

$newFlag = $template.'msPKI-Enrollment-Flag' -band (-bnot 0x80000)

Set-ADObject -Identity $template.DistinguishedName -Replace @{'msPKI-Enrollment-Flag' = $newFlag}

  1. Enforce strong certificate binding on all domain controllers by setting the StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement registry value to 2:

reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Kdc /v StrongCertificateBindingEnforcement /t REG_DWORD /d 2 /f

Restart the Key Distribution Center (KDC) service on each DC after applying this change.

  1. Review and restrict enrollment permissions on all affected templates. Open Certificate Templates (certtmpl.msc), right-click the template, select Properties, navigate to the Security tab, and remove enrollment rights for non-privileged groups such as Domain Users or Authenticated Users.

Indicators.Name: Smart card password rotation disabled
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks whether the msDS-ExpirePasswordsOnSmartCardOnlyAccounts attribute, which determines if smart card-only accounts must follow regular password rotation schedules, is disabled.
Indicators.Remediation: To remediate this security issue, enable the msDS-ExpirePasswordsOnSmartCardOnlyAccounts attribute by opening ADSIEdit.msc with an account that has domain administrative privileges. Connect to the Configuration naming context, navigate to the domain configuration object, right-click on the domain object, and select "Properties". Go to the "Attribute Editor" tab, locate the "msDS-ExpirePasswordsOnSmartCardOnlyAccounts" attribute, and change its value to "TRUE" (case-sensitive). Click "Apply" and then "OK" to save the changes.

Indicators.Name: FGPP not applied to Global group
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for FGPP targeted to a Universal or Domain Local group.
Indicators.Remediation: Confirm that the following groups should be Universal or Domain Local, otherwise change their scope settings to Global for FGPP to apply to them.

Indicators.Name: Foreign Security Principal in privileged group
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for Foreign Security Principals (FSPs) who are members of privileged groups. Special care should be taken when including accounts from other domains as members of privileged groups.
Indicators.Remediation: Validate whether this member should be a member of the privileged group.

Indicators.Name: gMSA not in use
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if there are enabled group Managed Service Account (gMSA) objects in the domain.
Indicators.Remediation: Group Managed Service Accounts should be used to protect service accounts. See description for more information.

Indicators.Name: gMSA object with old password
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for group managed service accounts that have not automatically rotated their passwords. These passwords should be changed automatically every 30 days by default.
Indicators.Remediation: Managed Service Accounts' passwords should be changed every 30 days. This is also the default setting. The returned accounts should be investigated for why their passwords were not changed. Note: The 'Active' column shows if the account was active in the past 45 days.

Indicators.Name: Non-privileged user with access to gMSA password
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for principals listed within MSDS-groupMSAmembership that are not in the built-in admin groups.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that there are no unnecessary principals who can read Group Managed Service Account passwords via the msDS-GroupMSAMembership attribute.

Indicators.Name: Writable shortcut in GPO
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for shortcuts within Group Policy Objects (GPOs) that are writable by low privilege users. GPOs are a powerful feature in Windows domains that are used to manage various settings and configurations for multiple computers and users. Shortcuts are links to files or applications that can be deployed using GPOs. When low privilege users have the ability to modify these shortcuts, it could potentially lead to security risks and unauthorized modifications. This indicator helps organizations to identify such misconfigurations and take appropriate actions.
Indicators.Remediation: It is crucial to review and adjust permissions on the identified writable shortcuts to ensure that only authorized users have the right access to them.

Indicators.Name: Risky GPO logon script path
Indicators.Description: This indicator searches for logon script paths where the script does not exist and where a low-privilege user has permissions on the parent folder. Additionally, it checks for logon script paths where the script exists but low-privilege users have permissions to modify them.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that the GPO logon script exists, and that the logon script path does not provide normal users with permissions to change the script file or access to their parent folder.

Indicators.Name: GPO permits reversible password encryption
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies Group Policy Objects (GPOs) that allow passwords to be stored using reversible encryption. This setting effectively stores passwords in a format that can be easily decrypted, similar to storing them in plaintext. While this configuration may be required in rare legacy authentication scenarios, it poses a significant security risk in most modern environments.
Indicators.Remediation:
Audit all Group Policy Objects (GPOs) in the environment and disable the "Store passwords using reversible encryption" setting unless absolutely required.

This setting can be found in Computer Configuration\Policies\Windows Settings\Security Settings\Account Policies\Password Policy.

If this setting is found enabled and not in active use, modify the GPO to disable it and consider resetting the passwords of affected accounts. Going forward, ensure that password policies enforce strong hashing and that no GPOs re-enable reversible encryption.

This includes disabled GPOs, as they can be accidentally re-enabled or copied into active policies, reintroducing the risk. Even if a GPO is not currently linked or enforced, insecure settings within it should still be corrected or the GPO should be deleted if no longer needed.

Indicators.Name: GPO with Scheduled Tasks configured
Indicators.Description: When a scheduled task launches an executable, it checks to see if low-privilege users have permissions to modify GPOs.
Indicators.Remediation: It is crucial to properly configure group policies with scheduled tasks and grant appropriate levels of access to users and groups in order to inhibit misuse and abuse.

Indicators.Name: GPO with unprivileged owner
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies Group Policy Objects (GPOs) that are owned by unprivileged accounts.
Indicators.Remediation: Review the ownership of all Group Policy Objects and transfer ownership of any GPOs owned by unprivileged accounts to a trusted administrative group, such as 'Domain Admins'.

Indicators.Name: Risky user permissions granted by GPO
Indicators.Description: Group Policy Objects (GPOs) are used to define security settings that apply to a group of users or computers in an Active Directory environment. GPOs can be used to grant dangerous user rights, such as the ability to bypass file system security, log on as a service, or even perform actions with elevated privileges. This indicator looks for non-privileged users who are granted elevated permissions through GPO.
Indicators.Remediation: The remediation for this indicator involves identifying any dangerous user rights that have been granted through GPOs, and removing them wherever possible. This can involve reviewing existing GPO settings and modifying them to remove any unnecessary or excessive user rights, as well as implementing appropriate access controls to restrict access to GPOs and other critical Active Directory components. By taking these steps, organizations can reduce the risk of compromise and help protect their systems from potential attacks.

Indicators.Name: GPO Weak LM Hash storage enabled
Indicators.Description: This indicator detects when the "Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change" Group Policy Object setting is disabled within the Windows operating system.
Indicators.Remediation:
Microsoft best practices for this value are:

  • Set Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change to Enabled.
  • Require all users to set new passwords the next time they sign in to the domain so that LAN Manager hashes are removed.

Indicators.Name: GPO with reversible password
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks the SYSVOL share for Group Policy Preference files that contain Cpassword entries - credentials stored using a fixed AES encryption key published by Microsoft.
Indicators.Remediation:
Treat any discovered Cpassword entry as a credential that must be considered fully compromised, as the AES encryption key is publicly known and the password can be recovered in milliseconds. Immediately reset the password for every account whose credentials appear in a Cpassword entry before removing the entry itself, to prevent an attacker who may have already harvested these credentials from using them after remediation.

To locate and remove the Cpassword entries:

  1. Open the Group Policy Management Console (gpmc.msc).
  2. Locate the GPO identified in the indicator results. Right-click the GPO and select Edit to open the Group Policy Management Editor.
  3. Navigate to the preference item containing the password. Common locations include:
    • Computer Configuration > Preferences > Control Panel Settings > Local Users and Groups
    • Computer Configuration > Preferences > Windows Settings > Drive Maps
    • Computer Configuration > Preferences > Control Panel Settings > Services
  4. Right-click the preference item containing the password and select Delete. Do not simply clear the password field, as the item may re-create a new Cpassword entry on next policy refresh.
  5. Confirm the change by running gpupdate /force on a target machine and verifying the GPO XML file in SYSVOL no longer contains a cpassword attribute.

Indicators.Name: Built-in guest account enabled
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if the built-in Active Directory "guest" account is enabled. The guest account allows for accounts with no password access to the domain and is disabled in most AD environments.
Indicators.Remediation: The guest account should be disabled to prevent the associated security risks.

Indicators.Name: Objects containing hidden Unicode characters
Indicators.Description: This indicator detects Active Directory objects that have "hidden" Unicode characters within their names.
Indicators.Remediation:
Detect and review the users by using the supplied information, such as DistinguishedName or ObjectSID.

This is an informational IoC. It does not provide strong evidence that a breach has occurred, but it does outline misconfigured users that should be examined. The higher severity version of this indicator is named "Suspicious duplicate objects using hidden Unicode characters".

Indicators.Name: Suspicious duplicate objects using hidden Unicode characters
Indicators.Description: This indicator detects Active Directory objects that mimic the appearance of other objects using "hidden" Unicode characters within their names.
Indicators.Remediation:
Detect and review the users by using the supplied information, such as DistinguishedName or ObjectSID.

This indicator finds suspicious "duplicate" objects, which could be indicative of a previous compromise. Examine the suspicious user and the original user, focusing on information such as:

  • Is the original user privileged or highly valuable?
  • When was the suspicious user created?
  • Who was the suspicious user created by?
  • Did the suspicious user perform actions that were missed because of hidden characters in its name?
  • Did the suspicious user inadvertently gain excess permissions because of hidden characters in its name?

If an object is determined as legitimate, consider removing the hidden characters or excluding it from the indicator.

Indicators.Name: Domain Controller not authenticated to the domain over 45 days
Indicators.Description: Domain Controllers must authenticate and change their passwords at least every 30 days. Lack of domain authentication reveals out-of-sync machines. Out-of-sync domain controllers must be either reinstalled or removed. When reinstalling an out-of-sync domain controller, care must be taken not to introduce a new OWNER control path exposing its computer account. To avoid doing so, use of the Djoin utility is advised.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that any DCs that have not been in communication with the domain for more than 30 days are either de-commissioned or re-promoted into the environment to ensure consistency with the production AD.

Indicators.Name: User with permission to set Server Trust Account
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for non-default principals that have the DS-Install-Replica extended right (Add/Remove Replica In Domain) on the domain naming context head. This permission allows a principal to set the SERVER_TRUST_ACCOUNT flag in the userAccountControl attribute of computer objects.
Indicators.Remediation:
Before remediating, investigate the identified principal's recent activities. Check Active Directory audit logs for any recent computer account creations or modifications to the userAccountControl attribute containing the SERVER_TRUST_ACCOUNT flag, as this may indicate an active compromise.

To remove the unnecessary permission:

  1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc).
  2. In the View menu, ensure Advanced Features is enabled.
  3. Right-click the domain object (the root node, e.g., DC=yourdomain,DC=com) and select Properties.
  4. Navigate to the Security tab and click Advanced.
  5. Locate the Access Control Entry (ACE) for the principal identified by the indicator. The permission may appear as Add/Remove Replica In Domain.
  6. Select the entry and click Remove to delete the permission, or click Edit to clear the specific Add/Remove Replica In Domain checkbox if it is bundled with other legitimate permissions.
  7. Click OK to apply the changes.

Ensure that this permission is strictly limited to authorized domain administrators or automated deployment accounts that genuinely require the ability to promote new Domain Controllers.

Indicators.Name: Kerberos krbtgt account with old password
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks the age of the password on the KRBTGT account.
Indicators.Remediation:
It is recommended that the KRBTGT account password is rotated at least once every 180 days.

Further, it recommended that the KRBTGT account password be rotated whenever a user with privileged access in Active Directory, such as a Domain Admin, leaves the organization.

There are certain considerations that must be taken into account to ensure a successful rotation of the password. FFor security purposes, the KRBTGT password must be changed twice to take full effect, and adequate time must be allowed for replication across all domain controllers. Improper timing or replication issues may affect the functionality and availability of Active Directory. Please refer to the reference article from Semperis for further details.

Indicators.Name: Non default value on ms-Mcs-AdmPwd SearchFlags
Indicators.Description: Some flags on the ms-Mcs-AdmPwd schema may inadvertently cause passwords to be visible to users allowing an attacker to use it as stealthy backdoor. This indicator looks for any changes to default searchFlags, which may create an exposure. Detection of changes to the default will result in a score of 80 for this indicator, signifying that a review should be conducted. Any removal of the default flags will result in a score of 0 due to their importance to security.
Indicators.Remediation: Investigate the change of the mc-Mcs-AdmPwd attribute searchFlags and change it back to the default (904).

Indicators.Name: LDAP channel binding not required on DCs
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for domain controllers where LDAP channel binding is not required.
Indicators.Remediation:
The steps to enforcing LDAP binding over SSL/TLS should be followed carefully so as to avoid disruptions in the domain (note that communication will fail with clients that don't send a CBT when performing LDAP binding over SSL/TLS).
  1. Before enabling LDAP channel binding on a domain controller, clients must install a security update as described in CVE-2017-8563.
  2. Require LDAP Channel Binding - Configure the Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options -> Domain Controller: LDAP server channel binding token requirements -> select Always in the dialog box.
    3. (Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\NTDS\Parameters' -Name LdapEnforceChannelBinding -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue).LdapEnforceChannelBinding
  3. A value of 2 indicates "Always", and confirms that the GPO is taking effect on that DC.

Indicators.Name: Query policy with LDAP deny list set
Indicators.Description: This security indicator is designed to check for LDAP IP deny lists across multiple domains in an Active Directory environment. For each available domain, it query the Active Directory for "query policies" associated with that domain, specifically looking for LDAP IP deny lists (ldapipdenylist attribute).
Indicators.Remediation:
