To mitigate potential security risks associated with the LDAP IP deny list, the following steps are recommended:
  1. Regular Audits: Conduct regular reviews of the LDAP IP deny list to ensure all entries are authorized and legitimate.
  2. Change Management: Implement strict change management procedures for modifications to the LDAP IP deny list. (Semperis DSP for example).
  3. Security Policy Violations: Entries that violate the organization's established security policies.
  4. Security Monitoring: Utilize security information and event management (SIEM) tools to monitor for unauthorized changes or access attempts blocked by the deny list.

Indicators.Name: LDAP signing not required on DCs
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for domain controllers where LDAP signing is not required.
Indicators.Remediation:
To remediate follow the steps below:

If the steps are not followed in order, disruption to Active Directory may occur.

  1. Configure clients to request LDAP signing. Group policy: Network security:LDAP client signing requirements, select Negotiate signing.
  2. When all clients request signing, configure domain controllers to require LDAP signing. Group policy: Domain Controller:LDAP server signing requirements, select Require signing.
  3. Configure clients to require LDAP signing. Group policy: Network security:LDAP client signing requirements, select Require signing.
  4. For full details on the process please see the reference articles.

Indicators.Name: GPO enforcing LLMNR
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if any Group Policy Objects (GPOs) explicitly enforce Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) settings via registry policy entries.
Indicators.Remediation:
To remediate GPOs that enforce LLMNR, begin by opening the Group Policy Management Console (GPMC) on a domain-joined management workstation or a domain controller. Identify the specific GPO that is applying the LLMNR configuration. Once located, follow these steps:

  • Right-click the GPO and select Edit to open the Group Policy Management Editor.
  • Navigate to: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client.
  • Double-click the setting named Turn off Multicast Name Resolution.
  • Change the setting to Enabled, then click Apply and OK.

After saving the changes, ensure the GPO is linked correctly to the desired organizational units (OUs) and that the affected systems are within scope.

Indicators.Name: Forest contains more than 50 privileged accounts
Indicators.Description: This indicator counts the number of privileged user accounts defined in the forest, where 50 is deemed the upper limit for these types of accounts. A privileged account is defined by its membership in designated privileged groups.
Indicators.Remediation: It's always best to keep the number of privileged accounts as low as possible. Consider using solutions that allow for Just-in-time administration or implement admin tiering to ensure that only certain accounts can access domain controller, workstation and server resources.

Indicators.Name: AD object created within the last 10 days
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for any AD objects that were created within the last 10 days. It is meant to be used for threat hunting, post-breach investigation or compliance validation.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that the new objects are known and legitimate.

Indicators.Name: Privileged account recently created
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for any users or groups that were created within the last month. Privileged accounts and groups are defined by having their adminCount attribute set to 1.
Indicators.Remediation: Review the list and verify that all privileged accounts and groups that were recently created are valid. Ideally, all privileged account creation goes through an approval-based workflow and gets periodic attestation.

Indicators.Name: Distributed COM Users or Performance Log Users not empty
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if either the Distributed COM Users group and/or Performance Log Users group in Active Directory are populated.
Indicators.Remediation:
Organizations should evaluate the use of these groups and restrict the membership of these groups to trusted users.

Organizations that are using these groups should implement an appropriate rights delegation to the necessary OUs in Active Directory as an alternative.

Indicators.Name: Schema Admins not empty
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if the Schema Admins group in Active Directory is populated.
Indicators.Remediation:
As membership in the Schema Admins group is not required for any purpose beyond making schema changes, it is recommended to remove all members of the group.

Only add accounts to the group when a change to the schema is required, and ensure those accounts are removed afterward.

Indicators.Name: Non-privileged account with adminCount=1
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for any users or groups that may have been under the control of SDProp (adminCount=1) but are no longer members of privileged groups and should not be considered privileged.
Indicators.Remediation: Remove the adminCount = 1 attribute from these users. Investigate unknown users with this attribute.

Indicators.Name: Unexpected principal with write access to sensitive GPO metadata attribute
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies unexpected users, groups, or computers with WriteProperty permissions to critical Group Policy Object (GPO) metadata attributes in Active Directory. It analyzes fine-grained ACEs to detect write access to attributes such as gPCFileSysPath, gPCMachineExtensionNames, gPCUserExtensionNames, and gPCWQLFilter.
Indicators.Remediation:
To fix these issues, you need to remove or adjust access control permissions on Group Policy Objects (GPOs) so that only trusted administrators can make changes to them. This can be done using the built-in Active Directory tools in Windows.

Follow these steps to review and fix permissions:

  • Open the Group Policy Management Console (run gpmc.msc from the Start menu or Run dialog).
  • In the left-hand pane, expand your forest and domain, then click on the Group Policy Objects folder.
  • Find the GPO you want to review. Right-click it and choose Edit to view its settings (optional), or choose Properties.
  • In the Properties window, go to the Delegation tab. This tab shows who has permissions to manage the GPO.
  • Click Advanced at the bottom-right to open the full permission list.
  • Review the entries for any users or groups that have permissions like Edit Settings or Write. No computer accounts should be under this tab.
  • Select any unknown or unnecessary accounts, and click Remove or Edit to reduce their access.
  • When done, click OK to apply changes.

After making these changes, click Apply and OK to save. Repeat the process for any other GPOs that may have risky permissions. This helps prevent unauthorized users from changing how policies behave or injecting malicious settings into your domain.

Indicators.Name: Unexpected principal with metadata edit permission on a GPO linked to a critical AD container
Indicators.Description: This indicator detects unexpected users, groups, or computers that have write access to critical GPO metadata attributes (such as script paths, extension execution, or WMI filters) on GPOs that are linked to sensitive Active Directory containers, such as the domain root, Domain Controllers OU, or Sites.
Indicators.Remediation:
Before modifying permissions, investigate the identified unexpected principal to determine if their account was recently compromised or if the metadata write permissions were maliciously added. Check directory audit logs for any recent modifications to the flagged GPO's attributes.

To revoke excessive metadata permissions and secure the GPO:

  1. Open the Group Policy Management Console (gpmc.msc).
  2. Navigate to Group Policy Objects, locate the affected GPO, right-click it, and select Properties.
  3. Go to the Delegation tab and click Advanced to view granular permissions.
  4. Locate the unexpected principal identified by the indicator. Remove any Write or Edit permissions on the AD object, ensuring the principal is restricted to Read-only access or removed entirely if no access is needed.
  5. Click OK to save the updated security descriptor.

Finally, review the GPO's links by selecting the GPO and viewing the Scope tab in the main GPMC window. If the GPO is no longer required at a highly sensitive scope (like the Domain root or Domain Controllers OU), right-click the link and select Delete to minimize the attack surface.

Indicators.Name: Unexpected principal that can edit GPOs
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for principals that are not members of the well-known builtin privileged groups that have any edit permissions on any GPO in the domain.
Indicators.Remediation:
In the Group Policy Management Console (GPMC), locate the target GPO and open the "Delegation" tab.

You will see a list of principals with delegation rights for that GPO.
The three default permissions are:

  • Read - Allows users to view the GPO settings
  • Edit settings - Allows users to edit the GPO settings themselves
  • Edit settings, delete, modify security - Allows users to edit GPO settings, delete it and modify the security settings (basically Full Control on the GPO)

These baseline permission sets cannot be removed; GPMC will automatically reinstate them if deleted. Additional permissions can only be layered on top.

To minimize risk, ensure that non-privileged principals are assigned "Read" permissions only.

Indicators.Name: Unexpected principal with edit permissions on a GPO linked to a critical AD container
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies unexpected principals with edit permissions on a Group Policy Object (GPO) linked to a critical Active Directory container, such as the domain root, Sites, or Domain Controllers OU.
Indicators.Remediation:
Before altering permissions, inspect the identified GPO for malicious settings such as unauthorized Scheduled Tasks, rogue Startup/Logon scripts, or modified User Rights Assignments. If suspicious configurations exist, conduct a full incident response investigation to determine whether the policy was maliciously deployed to the environment.

To view and restrict the delegation rights on the affected GPO:

  1. Open the Group Policy Management Console (gpmc.msc).
  2. In the console tree, navigate to the target GPO under Group Policy Objects and select it.
  3. Click the Delegation tab to view the list of principals with rights to the GPO.
  4. Identify the unexpected principal flagged by the indicator. Ensure their permission level is restricted to Read (which allows viewing settings without modification).
  5. If granular rights must be removed, click Advanced, locate the principal, and explicitly remove any excessive Write permissions on the Security tab. Click OK when finished.

Finally, select the Scope tab to review the GPO links. If the GPO does not legitimately need to be linked to high-impact levels such as the domain root (DC=domain,DC=com), Sites, or the Domain Controllers OU, right-click the link in the Links section and select Delete to minimize the attack surface.

Indicators.Name: Non-privileged principal able to set a service principal name
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for permissions that let non-privileged principals set the service principal name (SPN) of an identity object. Every identity class that can hold a service principal name is examined, not only user objects: users, inetOrgPerson objects, computers, managed service accounts, group managed service accounts and delegated managed service accounts.
Indicators.Remediation:
Note on patch availability: Microsoft has released a security update addressing the KerberLoss vulnerability (CVE-2026-25177) in March 2026. This indicator is unable to verify whether the patch has been applied to your domain controllers; however, the reported permissions should still be reviewed, as they may increase the potential attack surface.

Review each reported access control entry and determine whether it belongs to a delegation that is still required, such as a process that registers service principal names for database, web or management services, or a cluster or migration tool. Removing an entry that is still in use may break Kerberos authentication for the affected service, so validate the change on a test object or during a change window before applying it broadly.

  1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc) and check the Advanced Features option under View.
  2. Navigate to the reported object, right-click it and select Properties.
  3. Click the Security tab and select the reported principal in the Group or user names pane. If the permission entry isn't visible, locate it using the Advanced button below the pane.
  4. Remove the permission entry, or deselect the Allow checkbox for the reported permission, then click Apply.
  5. Reopen the Advanced security dialog on the object to confirm that the entry is gone, and confirm that the finding clears on the next scheduled scan.

When the permission is inherited, apply the change on the parent object that defines it, and verify the result on the child objects that received it.

When the result reports group(s) with more than 4500 transitive members, review the membership of those groups and keep only the objects that require the privilege. A secure environment should not have such a high number of privileged group members, and the members beyond that limit are not evaluated by this indicator.

When the result reports objects that could not be read during the group enumeration, check why they are hidden by the access control list of the object or of its organizational unit. The permissions those objects hold are not evaluated by this indicator until they can be read.

Delegation that is required for daily operations should be granted to dedicated administrative accounts that are monitored and protected, and should be scoped to the smallest possible set of objects. Accounts that hold a service principal name should use a long, randomly generated password, or be replaced by a group managed service account.

Indicators.Name: Non-privileged principal able to set a user principal name
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for permissions that let non-privileged principals set the user principal name (UPN) of an identity object. Every identity class that can hold a user principal name is examined, not only user objects: users, inetOrgPerson objects, computers, managed service accounts, group managed service accounts and delegated managed service accounts.
Indicators.Remediation:
Note on patch availability: Microsoft has released a security update addressing the ResetNightmare vulnerability (CVE-2026-27912) in April 2026. This indicator is unable to verify whether the patch has been applied to your domain controllers; however, the reported permissions should still be reviewed, as they may increase the potential attack surface.

Review each reported access control entry and determine whether it belongs to a delegation that is still required, such as an account provisioning process, an identity management or human resources connector, or a migration tool. Removing an entry that is still in use interrupts these processes, so validate the change on a test object or during a change window before applying it broadly.

  1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc) and check the Advanced Features option under View.
  2. Navigate to the reported object, right-click it and select Properties.
  3. Click the Security tab and select the reported principal in the Group or user names pane. If the permission entry isn't visible, locate it using the Advanced button below the pane.
  4. Remove the permission entry, or deselect the Allow checkbox for the reported permission, then click Apply.
  5. Reopen the Advanced security dialog on the object to confirm that the entry is gone, and confirm that the finding clears on the next scheduled scan.

When the permission is inherited, apply the change on the parent object that defines it, and verify the result on the child objects that received it.

When the result reports group(s) with more than 4500 transitive members, review the membership of those groups and keep only the objects that require the privilege. A secure environment should not have such a high number of privileged group members, and the members beyond that limit are not evaluated by this indicator.

When the result reports objects that could not be read during the group enumeration, check why they are hidden by the access control list of the object or of its organizational unit. The permissions those objects hold are not evaluated by this indicator until they can be read.

Delegation that is required for daily operations should be granted to dedicated administrative accounts that are monitored and protected, and should be scoped to the smallest possible set of objects.

Indicators.Name: Account with non-default PGID
Indicators.Description: This indicator returns a list of users and computers whose Primary Group IDs (PGIDs) are not the defaults for domain users and computers. Users created in the domain will have a default PGID of 513 (Domain Users) or 514 (Domain Guests) while computers are 515 (Domain Computers), 516 (Domain Controllers), or 521 (RODC). The Primary Group ID is not automatically changed when a user is moved to a different group (i.e. a user moved into Domain Admins will not be assigned PGID 512). This fact can be used to hide users with privileges to systems that rely on PGID, while hiding the user from queries that rely on enumerating the member attribute without the PGID. Additionally, group objects' member attribute will not list the user objects with PGID of those groups.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure these PGIDs are needed. When unneeded change the Primary Group to Domain Users (can be done through the MemberOf tab in dsa.msc).

Indicators.Name: Non-standard schema permissions
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for additional principals with permissions beyond generic Read to the schema partitions. Schema is one of three main Active Directory naming contexts. It contains every object attribute definition of the forest.
Indicators.Remediation: It is recommended to revert schema permissions to default state. See indicator description for additional info and link.

Indicators.Name: Account without readable PGID
Indicators.Description: This indicator finds users and computers for whom it can't read the PGID. This may be due to the default permission of Read access having been removed, which could indicate an attempt to hide the user (in combination with removal of the memberOf attribute).
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that these objects are known and legitimate and check their nTSecurityDescriptor to see if some ACE is causing the Primary Group ID attribute to be unreadable.

Indicators.Name: NTFRS SYSVOL Replication
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for indication of usage of FRS for sysvol replication. Domain Controllers are configured to use the NTFRS replication protocol (especially for SYSVOL replication). This protocol is obsolete and unnecessarily adds administrative interfaces to domain controllers. In addition, this protocol is no longer supported by the latest versions of Windows Server, which prevents migration to the latest versions.
Indicators.Remediation: This protocol is obsolete since Windows Server 2008.

Indicators.Name: Object with Reanimate-Tombstones extended right
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if there are any non-default principals with the Reanimate-Tombstones extended right configured.
Indicators.Remediation:
By default, only domain administrators can restore deleted objects, and it is not recommended to delegate the "Reanimate-Tombstones" right to other users since tombstone reanimation is a highly privileged and infrequent operation.

The "Reanimate Tombstone" control access right is granted at the Naming Context root. To remove the detected privilege assignments, perform the following steps:

  1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc) and check the Advanced Features option under View.
  2. Right-click the domain root object and select Properties to view its properties.
  3. Click the Security tab and select the detected object in the "Group or user names" pane.
  4. Scroll down in the permissions pane to locate the "Reanimate tombstones" permission entry. If the permission isn't visible, you may need to find it using the Advanced button below the pane.
  5. Deselect the "Allow" checkbox for the permission, then click Apply to save the change.

Indicators.Name: Object in privileged group without adminCount=1 (SDProp)
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for objects in privileged groups with AdminCount not equal to 1. AdminCount is an object flag that is set by the SDProp process (run by default every 60 minutes) if that object's DACLs are modified to sync with the AdminSDHolder object through inheritance. If an object within these groups has an AdminCount not equal to 1 then it could signify that the DACLs were manually set (no inheritance) or that there is an issue with SDProp.
Indicators.Remediation: Set adminCount=1 and ensure that SDProp is working properly.

Indicators.Name: Object with constrained delegation configured
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for any objects that have values in the msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo attribute (i.e. Constrained Delegation) and does not have the UserAccountControl bit for protocol transition set.
Indicators.Remediation: Validate that every delegation configured is known and necessary.

Indicators.Name: Principal with constrained authentication delegation enabled for a DC service
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for principals (computers or users) that have constrained delegation enabled for a service running on a DC. If an attacker can create such a delegation, they can authenticate to that service using any user that is not protected against delegation.
Indicators.Remediation: Remove any delegations, constrained or otherwise, that are defined against remote DC services.

Indicators.Name: Computer with exposed Microsoft LAPS password
Indicators.Description:
This indicator looks for permissions on computer accounts that could allow inadvertent exposure of local administrator account passwords in environments that use the legacy Microsoft Local Administrator Password Solution (Microsoft LAPS). These permissions include read access to the ms-Mcs-AdmPwd attribute, as well as Write DACL and Write Owner rights that would allow provisioning such access. Legacy Microsoft LAPS provides a method to rotate local administrator account passwords on servers and workstations by storing them in Active Directory.

Note: Legacy Microsoft LAPS is deprecated as of Windows 11 23H2 and later. If your environment supports it, consider migrating to Windows LAPS, the built-in successor available on Windows 10/11 and Windows Server 2019 and later (with the April 2023 update). See the companion indicator Changes to Windows LAPS read permissions for Windows LAPS coverage.
Indicators.Remediation:
Ensure that only authorized administrative principals have access to legacy Microsoft LAPS passwords on computer objects.

Review and restrict extended rights on the ms-Mcs-AdmPwd attribute. Remove any unnecessary principals with WriteDacl or WriteOwner rights on LAPS-managed computer objects, as these rights can be used to self-grant password read access.

Migration recommendation: Legacy Microsoft LAPS is deprecated on newer Microsoft OS versions (Windows 11 23H2 and later). Begin planning migration to Windows LAPS, which is natively available on Windows Server 2019 and later, and on Windows 10/11 with the April 2023 update. Windows LAPS offers significant improvements including:

  • Password encryption in Active Directory
  • Password history support
  • Microsoft Entra ID / Intune integration
  • DSRM account password management on domain controllers

Use the Update-LapsADSchema PowerShell cmdlet to extend the schema for Windows LAPS, and use Windows LAPS emulation mode to assist with the transition from legacy Microsoft LAPS.

Indicators.Name: Kerberos protocol transition delegation configured
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for services that have been configured to allow Kerberos protocol transition. This capability enables a delegated service to use any available authentication protocol. This means that compromised services can reduce the quality of their authentication protocol to something that is more easily compromised (e.g. NTLM).
Indicators.Remediation: Validate that every delegation configured is known and necessary. Check if constrained kerberos could be configured instead of protocol transition.

Indicators.Name: Principal with constrained delegation using protocol transition enabled for a DC service
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for principals (computers or users) that have constrained delegation using protocol transition defined against a service running on a DC.
Indicators.Remediation: Remove any delegations that are defined against remote DC services.

Indicators.Name: Computer with exposed Windows LAPS password
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for permissions on computer accounts that could allow inadvertent exposure of local administrator account passwords in environments that use Windows Local Administrator Password Solution (Windows LAPS). These permissions include read access to the msLAPS-Password attribute (clear-text mode) and the ms-LAPS-Encrypted-Password-Attributes extended right (encrypted mode), as well as Write DACL and Write Owner rights that would allow provisioning such access. Windows LAPS is the built-in successor to legacy Microsoft LAPS, available on Windows 10/11 and Windows Server 2019 and later following the April 2023 update.
Indicators.Remediation:
Ensure that only authorized administrative principals have access to Windows LAPS passwords on computer objects.

For clear-text mode deployments, review and restrict extended rights on the msLAPS-Password attribute. Use the Set-LapsADReadPasswordPermission PowerShell cmdlet to configure the authorized readers.

For encrypted mode deployments, review and restrict access granted via the ms-LAPS-Encrypted-Password-Attributes extended right (GUID: f3531ec6-6330-4f8e-8d39-7a671fbac605). Use the Set-LapsADReadPasswordPermission cmdlet accordingly.

Remove any unnecessary principals with WriteDacl or WriteOwner rights on Windows LAPS-managed computer objects, as these rights can be used to self-grant password read access.

Use the Windows LAPS PowerShell module (Get-LapsADPassword, Find-LapsADExtendedRights) to audit and manage delegated permissions.

Indicators.Name: High-privileged custom role
Indicators.Description: Custom roles were found that allow a user to perform actions on users' passwords. These custom roles grant elevated privileges and potentially pose a significant security risk if not properly managed.
Indicators.Remediation:
To mitigate the risks associated with high privilege custom roles, it is recommended to take the following actions:
  • Review and assess the necessity of the custom role. Ensure that the role is essential for specific business requirements and that it is not overly permissive.
  • Limit the assignment of the custom role to only those users who genuinely require these high privileges to perform their duties.
  • Regularly review and audit the membership of the custom role to ensure that it remains appropriate and necessary.
  • Implement the principle of least privilege by granting users only the minimum privileges necessary to perform their assigned tasks.
  • Monitor and log activities performed by users with high privilege roles to detect any suspicious or unauthorized actions.
By following these remediation steps, you can help reduce the potential risks associated with high privilege custom roles and enhance the security of your Okta environment.

Indicators.Name: New permission has been granted to a group
Indicators.Description: In the last 7 days, permission was given to a group.
Indicators.Remediation: Make sure that the permissions given to the group are indeed necessary and were done legitimately.

Indicators.Name: New permission has been granted to a user
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if any permissions have been granted to a user within the last 7 days.
Indicators.Remediation: Regularly review and validate the permissions assigned to users. Ensure that the permissions granted are necessary for their roles and responsibilities. Remove any unnecessary or excessive permissions to minimize the attack surface and maintain least privilege access control.

Indicators.Name: New API token was created
Indicators.Description: In the last 7 days,a new API token was created.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that the API token was created and used legitimately. Regularly review and audit API tokens to verify their necessity and permissions. Implement proper access controls and token management practices to mitigate the risk of unauthorized access.

Indicators.Name: New Super Admin permission has been granted to a group
Indicators.Description: In the last 7 days, "Super Admin" permission was given to a group.
Indicators.Remediation: Make sure that the "Super Admin" permissions given to the group are indeed necessary and were done legitimately.

Indicators.Name: New Super Admin permission has been granted to a user
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if the "Super Admin" permission was given to a user in the last 7 days.
Indicators.Remediation: Regularly review and audit the assignment of the "Super Admin" permission to ensure it is granted only when necessary and to authorized individuals. Implement strong access controls, such as multi-factor authentication and least privilege principles, to limit the impact of a compromised super admin account. Monitor and analyze user permission changes, and promptly investigate and address any unauthorized or suspicious activities related to the "Super Admin" permission.

Indicators.Name: Password policy check
Indicators.Description: This indicator evaluates the password policies in place and verifies if they adhere to Okta's recommendations.
Indicators.Remediation:
To ensure a robust password policy, please consider the following recommendations:
  • Set a password lockout threshold of 10 or more failed login attempts. This helps protect against brute-force password attacks.
  • Implement a minimum password history of 24 passwords. This prevents users from reusing previously compromised or weak passwords.
  • Establish a minimum password age of one hour. This ensures that users cannot immediately change their password to bypass the password history requirement.
  • Specify a minimum password length of 12 characters or more. Longer passwords offer increased resilience against brute-force attacks.
  • Consider restricting the use of common or easily guessable passwords, as recommended by Okta.

Indicators.Name: User activation in the last 7 days
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if a user has been activated within the last 7 days.
Indicators.Remediation: Review the activation status of users to confirm that they should indeed be active. Deactivate any users who no longer require access or whose activation may be unauthorized.

Indicators.Name: User deactivation in the last 7 days
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if a user has been deactivated within the last 7 days.
Indicators.Remediation: Review the deactivation status of users to confirm that they should indeed be deactivated. Reactivate any users who require access and whose deactivation may be unauthorized. Additionally, investigate any unauthorized deactivations as they may indicate malicious activity.

Indicators.Name: Users without Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks all users to identify those who have not registered for Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA).
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that MFA is enabled and enforced for all users.

Indicators.Name: User with old password
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for user accounts whose password has not changed in over 180 days. This could make these account ripe for password guessing attacks.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that users change their password at least once every 6 months.

Indicators.Name: Admin with old password
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for admin accounts whose password has not changed in over 180 days. This could make these accounts ripe for password guessing attacks.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that users change their password at least once every 6 months.

Indicators.Name: Operators group not empty
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if the Account Operators, Server Operators, Backup Operators and Print Operators groups in Active Directory are populated.
Indicators.Remediation:
Organizations should evaluate the use of these groups, and work to reduce and remove membership of these groups.

Organizations that are using these groups should implement an appropriate rights delegation to the necessary OUs in Active Directory as an alternative. For Backup Operators, organizations should implement a different group and manage access to lower tier servers or workstations through group policy objects.

If the organization accepts the risk of these groups being populated, they should use attack path analysis software, such as Forest Druid, to determine the attack paths that exist due to the population of these groups, and further consider members of this group to be Tier 0.

Indicators.Name: Outbound forest trust with SID History enabled
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for outbound forest trusts that have the TRUST_ATTRIBUTE_TREAT_AS_EXTERNAL flag set to true.
Indicators.Remediation:
Unless a forest migration is currently ongoing, use the following command to disable SIDHistory for the trust: NETDOM TRUST <ForestName> /domain:<TrustedForest> /EnableSIDHistory no

Organizations should understand the risk of leaving this enabled for an extended period of time.

Indicators.Name: Domain trust to a third-party domain without quarantine
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for outbound forest trusts that has Quarantine flag set to false, which means that the trusted domain is not subject to SID filtering.
Indicators.Remediation:
Unless domain migration is currently ongoing, use the following command to enable Quarantine for external trusts: NETDOM TRUST /domain: /Quarantine yes

And use the following command to disable SID history for forest trusts: NETDOM TRUST /domain: /EnableSIDHistory:No

Indicators.Name: Risky Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access Group membership
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for risky members (Everyone, Anonymous Logon, or Authenticated Users) in the built-in group "Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access", which grants read-only access to Active Directory.
Indicators.Remediation: Confirm that any addition or removals from Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access group are valid and properly accounted for.

Indicators.Name: User with SPN defined
Indicators.Description: This indicator provides a way to visually inventory all users accounts that have SPNs defined. Generally SPNs are only defined for "Kerberized" services, so if you see an account with an SPN that should not have one, this could be cause for concern.
Indicators.Remediation: If possible use Group Managed Service Accounts instead of regular users or ensure that all users that have an SPN are not primary users and considered as service accounts.

Indicators.Name: Primary user with SPN not supporting AES encryption on Kerberos
Indicators.Description: This indicator shows all Primary users with SPNs that do not support AES-128 or AES-256 encryption type.
Indicators.Remediation: Best practice is to enable AES encryption support on service accounts.

Indicators.Name: Privileged group membership changes in the last 7 days
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for changes to the built-in privileged groups within the last 7 days, which could indicate attempts to escalate privilege.
Indicators.Remediation: Confirm that any additions/removals from privileged groups are valid and properly accounted for.

Indicators.Name: Privileged user with a roaming profile
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for privileged accounts with a roaming profile configured on the user account (via the profilePath attribute). A roaming profile is a user profile stored on a network server that follows the user across different machines, allowing them to access the same desktop environment, settings, and files regardless of which computer they log in to. The profile is downloaded when the user logs in and synchronized back to the server when they log out. Additionally, roaming profiles are cached locally on each machine the privileged account logs in to, potentially exposing administrative credentials or sensitive data if those machines are compromised.
Indicators.Remediation:
Remove roaming profile configurations from all privileged accounts. Privileged accounts should use local profiles and only log in to administrative workstations. Create and enforce GPOs that explicitly prevent roaming profiles for privileged security groups.

To disable roaming profiles for privileged accounts through group policy, begin by opening the Group Policy Management Console on a domain controller or management workstation with the Remote Server Administration Tools installed. Create a new Group Policy specifically for privileged account restrictions, or modify an existing administrative account policy. It's recommended to create a dedicated GPO for this purpose to maintain clean policy separation and easier troubleshooting. Navigate to the Computer Configuration section, then proceed to Policies, followed by Administrative Templates, System, and finally User Profiles. Within this location, locate the policy setting named "Prevent Roaming Profile changes from propagating to the server" and enable it. This prevents any changes made to the roaming profile from being written back to the profile server. However, the more effective approach is to prevent the roaming profile from being loaded entirely. To completely disable roaming profile usage, you should configure the policy "Do not detect slow network connections" and also enable "Delete cached copies of roaming profiles" if you want to remove any existing cached profiles. However, the critical configuration involves preventing the roaming profile from being specified in the first place at the user account level. Open Active Directory Users and Computers, locate each privileged account, access the account properties, and navigate to the Profile tab. Ensure that the "Profile path" field is completely empty. This is the definitive method to prevent roaming profile usage for these accounts.

Review authentication logs for these accounts, looking for unusual login patterns, geographic anomalies, or access to unexpected systems. If suspicious activity is detected, treat it as a potential breach and initiate incident response procedures. In the long term, consider implementing dedicated, hardened workstations (PAWs) for administrative tasks with local profiles only. It's also recommended to separate privileged accounts by access tiers (Tier 0 for domain controllers, Tier 1 for servers, Tier 2 for workstations) and prevent cross-tier credential use.

Indicators.Name: Privileged user with SPN defined
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for accounts with the adminCount attribute set to 1 AND ServicePrincipalNames (SPNs) defined on the account. In general, privileged accounts should not have SPNs defined on them, as it makes them targets for Kerberos-based attacks that can elevate privileges to those accounts. By default, the krbtgt account falls under this category but is a special case and is not considered part of this indicator.
Indicators.Remediation: Remove SPN from privileged accounts when not required or mitigate by other means.

Indicators.Name: Privileged user with weak password policy
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for privileged users in each domain that do not have a strong password policy enforced via either the default domain password policy or a Fine-Grained Password Policy (FGPP).
Indicators.Remediation:
Before applying a stronger policy, investigate if the weak policy was deliberately targeted. Review sign-in logs and Active Directory authentication events for the flagged privileged users to identify any anomalous access patterns that might indicate existing compromise.

To enforce a stronger password policy for privileged accounts using a Fine-Grained Password Policy (FGPP):

  1. Open the Active Directory Administrative Center (dsac.exe).
  2. In the left navigation pane, select the domain, then navigate to System > Password Settings Container.
  3. Right-click the container, select New, and then click Password Settings.
  4. Provide a name for the policy and configure strong settings (e.g., minimum password length of 15 characters, enforce password history, and set a reasonable maximum password age).
  5. Under the Directly Applies To section, click Add and specify the privileged users or the administrative groups they belong to.
  6. Click OK to apply the policy.

Ensure that the affected privileged users reset their passwords immediately to comply with the newly applied strong policy.

Indicators.Name: Protected Users group not in use
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if privileged users are in the Protected Users security group.
Indicators.Remediation:
It is recommended to ensure that all privileged users are members of the Protected Users security group.

If the organization is already using the Protected Users security group functionality, it is recommended to add the identified privileged users.

If the Active Directory schema is pre Server 2012 R2, this functionality does not exist, and it is recommended to upgrade the schema.

For full details on the protections offered and the implementation of the Protected Users security group, please refer to the reference article.

Indicators.Name: Computer account takeover through Kerberos resource-based constrained delegation
Indicators.Description: With sufficient permissions on a computer account and the ability to create another user or computer security principal, it is possible to compromise resources on that computer account using Kerberos resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD). This indicator looks for the msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute on computer objects.
Indicators.Remediation: Validate Kerberos resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD) use requirements and ensure that any credential delegation observed is legitimate and expected.

Indicators.Name: Domain Controller with resource-based constrained delegation enabled
Indicators.Description: This indicator detects a configuration that grants certain accounts with complete delegation to domain controllers. Delegations towards privileged resources such as DCs should be avoided. Resource-based constrained delegation is configured on the target resource, as opposed to other delegation types that are configured on the accounts accessing the resource.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that the msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute on any DC is empty - this is the normal state for a DC.

Indicators.Name: krbtgt account with Resource-Based Constrained Delegation enabled
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if the krbtgt (Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket) account has Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) defined.
Indicators.Remediation:
There is no valid, non-malicious reason to configure Resource-Based Constrained Delegation on the krbtgt account. Treat this finding as a high-confidence Indicator of Compromise. Before removing the configuration, investigate Kerberos authentication logs for anomalous Ticket Granting Service (TGS) requests involving the principal trusted by the delegation, as this indicates active exploitation.

To remove the delegation, run the following command from an elevated PowerShell session with the Active Directory module loaded:

Set-ADUser krbtgt -PrincipalsAllowedToDelegateToAccount $null

Indicators.Name: Write access to RBCD on DC
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for write access on RBCD for Domain Controllers to users who are not in Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins and Built-in Admins groups.
Indicators.Remediation: For each DC listed, ensure that the principals who can set resource-based constrained delegation are valid.

Indicators.Name: Write access to RBCD on krbtgt account
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for Write access on RBCD for the krbtgt account to users who are not in Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins and Built-in Admins groups.
Indicators.Remediation: Review the list and ensure that there are no unnecessary principals who can set resource-based constrained delegation on krbtgt.

Indicators.Name: AZUREADSSOACC supporting RC4 or DES encryption
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if RC4 or DES encryption is supported by the SSO computer account, AZUREADSSOACC.
Indicators.Remediation:
Entra Seamless SSO supports the AES256_HMAC_SHA1, AES128_HMAC_SHA1 and RC4_HMAC_MD5 encryption types for Kerberos.

For security reasons, it is recommended that the encryption type for the AZUREADSSOACC account is set to one or both of the AES types and not RC4.

The encryption type is stored in the msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes attribute of the account in Active Directory, and if the value is empty (the default setting), Kerberos tickets will default to using RC4.

To change the attribute to a secure value, perform the following steps:

  1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc), and check the Advanced Features option under View.
  2. Navigate to the location of the AZUREADSSOACC account and double-click it to view its properties.
  3. Click the Attribute Editor tab and scroll down to find the msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes attribute.
  4. Double-click the attribute and set it to one of the secure supported values:
    • 8 (AES128_HMAC_SHA1)
    • 16 (AES256_HMAC_SHA1)
    • 24 (AES128_HMAC_SHA1 & AES256_HMAC_SHA1)
  5. Finally, ensure to roll over the Kerberos decryption key of the AZUREADSSOACC account as explained in Microsoft Entra seamless single sign-on: Frequently asked questions | Microsoft Learn, otherwise Seamless SSO will not work.

Indicators.Name: Domain Controller supporting RC4 or DES encryption
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if RC4 or DES encryption is supported by Domain Controllers
Indicators.Remediation:
It is best practice to disable support for RC4 and DES on domain controllers. Proceed with caution, as this can cause clients that request RC4 encrypted Kerberos tickets by default to fail.

To disable RC4 and DES encryption:

  1. Open Group Policy Management Console
  2. Navigate to a GPO that affects the Domain Controllers container
  3. Go to Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options
  4. Find the policy Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos
  5. Enable the policy and select only AES-128 and AES-256 encryption types
  6. Apply the GPO and allow time for replication

Indicators.Name: Objects with recent SIDHistory changes
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for any recent changes to SIDHistory on objects.
Indicators.Remediation:
If the identified SID is known due to efforts such as migration, ensure that it is known and documented, and also understand the risk involved of retaining this SIDHistory.

If the identified SID is unknown and there is not a clear chain of ownership of the change, the user identified should be treated as highly suspicious, as this may be a strong sign of a compromise of Active Directory. Organizations should start further investigation into the integrity of their Active Directory.

Indicators.Name: Non-default principal with DCSync rights on the domain
Indicators.Description: This indicator detects non-default principals that have directory replication permissions (Replicating Directory Changes, Replicating Directory Changes All) or the ability to grant these permissions (Write DACL, Owner) on the domain naming context object.
Indicators.Remediation:
Before revoking permissions, investigate the principal identified. If it is an unexpected account, review network traffic and Active Directory audit logs for signs of unauthorized replication activity mimicking Domain Controllers, as this may indicate an active DCSync attack.

To safely remove these permissions:

  1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc).
  2. In the View menu, ensure Advanced Features is enabled.
  3. Right-click the domain object (the root node, e.g., DC=yourdomain,DC=com) and select Properties.
  4. Navigate to the Security tab and click Advanced to view the advanced security settings.
  5. Locate the Access Control Entries (ACEs) belonging to the non-default principal.
  6. Select the entry that grants Replicating Directory Changes and/or Replicating Directory Changes All and click Remove. If the rights are combined with other necessary permissions, click Edit and uncheck those specific replication permissions.
  7. Click OK to apply the changes.

Note: Under certain architectures (e.g., Microsoft PAM/ESAE Tiering), an empty group or specific service account may legitimately require these permissions. Ensure you consult with architectural owners before removing them.

Indicators.Name: Risky RODC credential caching
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks the password replication policy on RODCs.
Indicators.Remediation:
It is recommended to adjust the password replication policy on the RODC to deny replication of privileged user credentials to an RODC.

You can review the current settings by opening Active Directory Users and Computers, locate the identified RODC, and then right-click and select Properties.

In the Properties of the RODC, select the Password Replication Policy tab.

Review the replication policies, identify the policy that is permitting replication of credentials, and adjust to ensure there is a deny policy for the privileged users.

You may also need to review the membership of the group Denied RODC Password Replication Group, which by default holds many privileged user groups that should be denied replication.

Indicators.Name: Privileged user credentials cached on RODC
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for privileged user credentials that are cached to RODCs.
Indicators.Remediation:
It is recommended to adjust the password replication policy on the RODC to deny replication of credentials for the identified privileged users.

You can review the current settings by opening Active Directory Users and Computers, locate the identified RODC, and then right-click and select Properties.

In the Properties of the RODC, select the Password Replication Policy tab.

Review the replication policies, identify the policy that is permitting replication of credentials, and adjust to ensure there is a deny policy for the privileged users.

Indicators.Name: Shadow credentials on privileged object
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for users with write access to the msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute of privileged users and DCs.
Indicators.Remediation:
Review the list of users who have write access to the msDS-KeyCredentialLink attribute on privileged objects.

Remove unnecessary write permissions for users who do not require this access for legitimate administrative purposes.

Indicators.Name: Principal with well-known privileged SID in SIDHistory
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks the sIDHistory attribute of security principals for well-known privileged SIDs (such as Domain Admins or Enterprise Admins).
Indicators.Remediation:
Because injecting a SID into the same domain requires Domain Admin-level privileges, you should treat this finding as a high-confidence Indicator of Compromise. Before removing the attribute, investigate the account's recent authentication history and audit logs to determine how and when the SID was injected, and what actions the attacker performed.

To safely clear the malicious sIDHistory entry, use PowerShell on a Domain Controller or a machine with RSAT installed:

  1. Open an elevated PowerShell prompt.
  2. To completely clear all SIDs from the account's history, run:

Get-ADUser "TargetUsername" -properties sidhistory | foreach {Set-ADUser $_ -remove @{sidhistory=$_.sidhistory.value}}

  1. If you need to remove a specific malicious SID while retaining legitimate migration SIDs, use:

Set-ADUser -Identity "TargetUsername" -Remove @{sIDHistory="S-1-5-21-Malicious-SID"}

Indicators.Name: User account using Smart Card authentication with old password
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for user accounts that are using Smart Card authentication whose password has not changed in the last 90 days.
Indicators.Remediation:
Implement regular password changes for users. Additionally, for Windows 2016 or later domains, leverage the msDS-ExpirePasswordsOnSmartCardOnlyAccounts attribute to enforce periodic password hashing even for smart card users. This enhances security by mitigating the risk associated with static password hashes.

To enable this attribute, use the following command (to enable the attribute msDS-ExpirePasswordsOnSmartCardOnlyAccounts):

Set-ADDomain -Identity DomainName -PublicKeyRequiredPasswordRolling $True

Indicators.Name: Domain controller without SMB signing required
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies domain controllers that do not strictly require SMB signing for incoming connections.
Indicators.Remediation:
Before enforcing SMB signing, verify that all legacy clients and critical appliances in the environment support signed SMB communications, as enforcing this setting will immediately block incoming SMB traffic from unsupported devices.

To enforce SMB signing network-wide via Group Policy:

  1. Open the Group Policy Management Console (gpmc.msc).
  2. Right-click the Default Domain Controllers Policy (or the specific GPO governing your DCs) and select Edit.
  3. Navigate to Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options.
  4. Locate the policy: Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always).
  5. Double-click the policy, check Define this policy setting, select Enabled, and click OK.

Allow time for Group Policy to refresh across the domain controllers, or force it manually by running gpupdate /force on the affected servers.

Indicators.Name: Domain controller with SMBv1 enabled
Indicators.Description: This indicator detects domain controllers where the legacy SMBv1 protocol is enabled.
Indicators.Remediation:
Before disabling SMBv1, ensure no mission-critical legacy devices (such as old multi-function network printers, legacy NAS appliances, or extremely outdated OS variants like Windows XP/2003) actively rely on it to communicate with the domain controller. If such devices exist, they should be upgraded or replaced immediately.

To disable the SMBv1 protocol on the domain controller:

  1. Open an elevated PowerShell prompt on the target Domain Controller.
  2. Run the following command to completely disable the server-side SMBv1 protocol:

Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false -Force

  1. To additionally ensure the legacy SMBv1 features are uninstalled from the OS entirely, run:

Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol -NoRestart

  1. Reboot the domain controller for the changes to fully take effect.

Indicators.Name: SYSVOL executable changes
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for modifications to executable files within SYSVOL. It only examines files and executables that have read access to them.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure all recently created/modified executables are safe.

Indicators.Name: Trust account with old password
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for trust accounts whose password has not changed within the last year. This could mean that a trust relationship was removed but its corresponding trust account wasn't cleaned up.
Indicators.Remediation: Old passwords on trust accounts usually indicate the trust is no longer valid. Verify that the trust account is no longer needed and then delete it.

Indicators.Name: Non-privileged principal as DNS Admins
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for members of the DnsAdmins group that are not members of any other built-in privileged groups.
Indicators.Remediation: Remove unprivileged principals that are members of the DNS Admins group, and ensure all Domain Controllers are fully up-to-date with the latest security updates from Microsoft.

Indicators.Name: Privileged object with unprivileged owner
Indicators.Description: If a privileged object (as determined by adminCount=1) is owned by an account that is unprivileged, then any compromise of that unprivileged account could result in those privileged objects' delegation being modified, since owners can override any delegation on an object, if only temporarily.
Indicators.Remediation: Remove unprivileged owner from privileged objects.

Indicators.Name: Unprotected privileged account can be delegated
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for Administrators who are not members of the Protected Users group and are not marked as sensitive for delegation.
Indicators.Remediation:
This indicator checks privileged accounts of various types. The security recommendations also vary depending on the type of accounts that were detected:

  • For user accounts, you can either enable the Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated option on the user object via Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc), or add the user to the Protected Users group to apply all of the group's security controls on it.
    As these accounts are already members of highly privileged groups, it is recommended to not add them to the Protected Users group until you can guarantee adding them won't have negative consequences. To read more about this, refer to the links provided in the References section.
  • Service accounts and machine accounts should not be added to the Protected Users group. To protect these objects, open Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc) and check the Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated option in the account's Account tab.

Indicators.Name: UPN or SPN uniqueness verification is disabled
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks if verification of uniqueness for user principal names, service principal names, or service principal name aliases is disabled.
Indicators.Remediation:
Verification of uniqueness for user principal name, service principal name, and service principal name aliases should be enabled to prevent environment-wide errors and increase security.

To enable uniqueness verification checks, edit the dSHeuristics attribute of the object CN=Directory Service,CN=Windows NT,CN=Services,CN=Configuration,DC=<forest_name>, and set its 21st character to 0, or truncate the string as needed. For more information, please follow Microsoft's detailed guides on the dSHeuristics attribute and uniqueness verification.

Indicators.Name: User with userPassword attribute
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for the attribute of userPassword existing on accounts.
Indicators.Remediation: It is recommended to remove the value from this attribute on all found users, Unless required by the environment.

Indicators.Name: Non-privileged user can add computer accounts to the domain
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for an AD configuration that allows unprivileged domain members to add computer accounts to the domain. By default, members of the Authenticated Users group can add up to 10 machine accounts to a domain. If the ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota attribute on the domain naming context head is not set to 0, regular users have this ability.The ability to do this confers certain rights on those created machine accounts that can be abused by a variety of Kerberos-based attacks. Note: This configuration may be enabled but be already mitigated by GPO settings (User Right: "Add workstations to domain" configured with only high-privileged group(s)/account(s)) linked to Domain Controllers OU that are not checked by this indicator.
Indicators.Remediation: Set the ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota attribute on the domain NC head to 0 to disable regular users' ability to add computer accounts.

Indicators.Name: User account using DES encryption
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies user accounts with the "Use Kerberos DES encryption types for this account" flag set. DES is an older cipher with a 56-bit key length that is relatively easy to crack. The only legitimate use for this flag is to support older systems and environments that only support DES.
Indicators.Remediation:
Disable the "Use Kerberos DES encryption types for this account" flag on all user accounts unless absolutely required for compatibility with legacy systems. Instead, ensure accounts are using stronger encryption types such as AES-256 or AES-128.

If DES support is unavoidable, ensure that affected accounts are assigned the least privileges necessary and are subject to strict monitoring for signs of abuse or unusual authentication behavior.

Indicators.Name: User with Password never expires flag
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies user accounts where the Password Never Expires flag is set. These accounts can be targets for brute force password attacks, given that their passwords may not be strong when they were set. These accounts also tend to be service accounts with privileged access to applications and services, including Kerberos-based services.
Indicators.Remediation: Move any user accounts away from Password Never Expires by having a good password rotation scheme and ensure any accounts that require this flag have the least privileges required. If this is a service account, considering using Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA).

Indicators.Name: Privileged account with password never expires flag
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies privileged accounts (adminCount attribute set to 1) where the Password Never Expires flag is set.
Indicators.Remediation: Enforce that users with privileged access must change their passwords on a regular basis and ensure that those passwords are complex and ideally require MFA to authenticate.

Indicators.Name: User account with password not required
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies user accounts that do not require a password.
Indicators.Remediation: Review and disable the "Password Not Required" flag for all user accounts unless it is explicitly required for operational reasons. In such cases, ensure the accounts are assigned the least privileges possible, are non-interactive where applicable, and are closely monitored for unusual activity.

Indicators.Name: User password stored with reversible encryption
Indicators.Description: This indicator looks for user accounts with the ENCRYPTED_TEXT_PWD_ALLOWED flag enabled. The secure way of storing passwords is by utilizing one-way encryption where it is mathematically impossible to derive the original password from the ciphertext. This setting encrypts the source password such that it is possible to derive the original. This setting is used when an application or service utilizes authentication protocols that require the original password, e.g. CHAP or IAS.
Indicators.Remediation: This flag represents a potential weakness in user accounts, which if left in place, could make these accounts targets of takeover attacks. It is strongly advised to disable reversible encryption if no service explicitly requires it. If the flag is required, ensure that these accounts have the least privileges possible and are closely monitored.

Indicators.Name: User with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled
Indicators.Description: This indicator identifies users with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled, which exposes them to potential ASREP-Roasting attacks, such as 'Kerberoasting'.
Indicators.Remediation: Ensure that pre-authentication is enabled on all users if possible; if not possible, consider reducing their privileges instead.

Indicators.Name: Certificate with weak cipher or small key size
Indicators.Description: This indicator detects certificates stored in Active Directory that utilize weak cryptography, such as a key size smaller than 2048 bits or the outdated DSA encryption algorithm.
Indicators.Remediation:
Before revoking, identify the systems or users relying on the problematic certificate to minimize authentication failures or service disruption during the replacement process.

To remediate the vulnerable certificate:

  1. Access the certificate enrollment system or the endpoint that issued the certificate.
  2. Generate a new Certificate Signing Request (CSR) ensuring modern cryptographic settings are strictly enforced (e.g., Use RSA or ECDSA signatures—do not use DSA—with a minimum RSA key size of 2048 bits).
  3. Issue and deploy the new, robust certificate to the required Active Directory objects or endpoints.
  4. Open the Certification Authority console (certsrv.msc) on the issuing CA.
  5. Locate the Issued Certificates folder.
  6. Right-click the weak certificate, select All Tasks, and click Revoke Certificate to permanently invalidate it.

Indicators.Name: GPO linking delegation at the AD Site level
Indicators.Description: When non-privileged users can link GPOs at the AD Site level, they have the ability to effect change on domain controllers as well as potentially elevate access and change domain-wide security posture. This indicator looks for non-default principals who have write permissions on the GPLink attribute or Write DACL/Write Owner on the object.
Indicators.Remediation: Unprivileged users should not be able to link GPOs at the AD Site Level. Doing so essentially gives them the ability to escalate their access, change domain-level security posture, and use GPOs to effect all systems and users in AD. Remove unnecessary permissions from the AD Site.

Indicators.Name: GPO linking delegation at the domain controller OU level
Indicators.Description: When non-privileged users can link GPOs at the Domain Controllers OU level, they have the ability to effect change on domain controllers as well as potentially elevate access and change domain-wide security posture. This indicator looks for non-default principals who have write permissions on the GPLink attribute or Write DACL/Write Owner on the object.
Indicators.Remediation: Unprivileged users should not be able to link GPOs at the Domain Controllers OU level. Doing so essentially gives them the ability to escalate their access, change domain-level security posture, and use GPOs to effect all systems and users in AD. Remove unnecessary permissions from the DC OU.

Indicators.Name: GPO linking delegation at the domain level
Indicators.Description: When non-privileged users can link GPOs at the domain level, they have the ability to effect change across all users and computers in the domain as well as potentially elevate access and change domain-wide security posture. This indicator looks for non-default principals who have write permissions on the GPLink attribute or Write DACL/Write Owner on the object.
Indicators.Remediation: Unprivileged users should not be able to link GPOs at the domain object level. Doing so essentially gives them the ability to escalate their access, change domain-level security posture, and use GPOs to effect all systems and users in AD. Remove the unnecessary permissions from the NC Head.

Indicators.Name: Zerologon vulnerability
Indicators.Description: This indicator checks for security vulnerability CVE-202-1472.
Indicators.Remediation: It is critical to ensure that the indicated domain controllers are patched for CVE-2020-1472, and have been restarted after the patch has been applied.
